#4937. Healthy on the Outside: The Silent Risk Dr. Nancy Snyderman Never Saw Coming

Nancy L. Snyderman, MD, spent decades helping millions of Americans understand their health. But when it came to her own health, it was a nudge from a friend that finally pushed her to get the care she really needed.

Nancy L. Snyderman, MD, began her career caring for one patient at a time. After medical school, Nancy became a board-certified surgeon, working at academic medical centers, and she kept running into the same gap: the distance between what doctors knew and what patients actually understood about their own health. Television, she realized, could help close it. “A big part of being a doctor, for me, was putting humanity back into medicine,” she says. So she traded caring for one patient at a time for caring for all Americans.

For nearly three decades, Americans welcomed Nancy into their homes through their televisions. As a chief medical correspondent, she covered wide ranging medical topics and traveled the world extensively, reporting from many of the world’s most-troubled areas. Every day, she expertly translated complex medical news into easily digestible—and actionable—information for people across America.

“I spent my whole career being the person who talked about health to help others,” she says. “I never thought I’d be the one in need of help.”

Nancy has always been active. Even now, she hikes, travels and keeps up with her young grandchildren. But being active and feeling good doesn’t always mean you’re healthy. No one knows this better than Nancy, who had no symptoms of heart disease before her diagnosis. It started when she was still a national medical correspondent, working on a story on CT angiograms and a then-new test that provided a coronary artery calcium (CAC) score. As part of her report, Nancy had the scan done herself and her score came back at 100. “I thought, ‘Oh my gosh, this is great, I aced this test’,” she says—only to learn that acing it means a score of zero.

What is a CAC Scan?A coronary artery calcium (CAC) scan is an imaging test that measures the amount of calcified plaque built up in the heart's arteries.1 It can help doctors and patients understand cardiovascular risk—even before symptoms appear.1

At the same time, she was struggling to keep her LDL-C, or low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, often called “bad” cholesterol, in check. High LDL-C is one of the leading risk factors for a heart attack or stroke, but also one of the most modifiable.2 To lower her LDL-C, Nancy had been taking statins—which are a commonly prescribed class of LDL-C lowering medication—for decades. “I knew what to do, and I thought I was doing the right things,” she says. “But I was never able to really get my bad cholesterol to my doctor-recommended level.”

What finally changed everything was a conversation. After reconnecting with an old friend, who also happens to be a cardiac nurse, Nancy mentioned her CAC score and stubborn LDL-C. Her friend insisted that Nancy see a new cardiologist. After some additional testing, the results were nothing Nancy ever expected to hear: severe coronary artery disease, with significant blockages in the arteries feeding her heart.

What is LDL-C?LDL-C stands for low-density lipoprotein cholesterol—often called “bad” cholesterol. When too much of it builds up in the blood, it can settle into artery walls, narrowing them and raising the risk of a heart attack or stroke over time.2

“My diagnosis was a huge wake-up call,” she says. “I thought I was doing the right things, but even I, as a physician, needed an advocate.” She’s quick to point out why that mattered: “A lot of the risks women face with heart disease can be managed,” she adds, “but only if we understand them and speak up for ourselves.”

Nancy’s experience is far more common than many women realize. Heart disease remains the leading cause of death for women in the United States3—yet only about half (56%) of women recognize it as their number one threat.3 “One of the most dangerous things about heart disease is how quietly it can develop,” says Sirisha Vadali, MD, a board-certified cardiologist in Scottsdale, Arizona. “It can progress silently, even when you feel completely healthy,4 and women in particular may not have the obvious warning signs we’ve all been taught to watch for.”

So much of that hidden risk traces back to a single number: LDL-C. When there’s too much of this “bad” cholesterol circulating, it doesn’t just sit in the blood. It works its way into the artery walls and builds up as a sticky plaque, narrowing them and raising the risk of a heart attack or stroke over time.5,6 “It isn’t only how high your LDL-C is today,” Dr. Vadali says. “It’s how high it has been, and for how long. The longer it’s too high, the more cardiovascular risk accumulates.”⁵

For Nancy, the lesson was humbling: expertise is not immunity. “You can be the most informed person in the room and still miss a health warning in yourself,” she says. It sometimes takes a push from a loved one to take the necessary action.

After her diagnosis, Nancy did exactly what she had spent years urging her viewers to do: she partnered with her cardiologist and built a plan. Together, they assessed her individual risk factors and set a clear target for her LDL-C to help lower her cardiovascular risk.

Getting there was more challenging than Nancy realized. “Despite standard treatment, diet, and exercise, my LDL-C was still too high, and we needed to lower it to my doctor-recommended LDL-C goal,” she says.

That gap—between lower and a guideline-recommended target—is one Dr. Vadali sees constantly. “When it comes to LDL-C, lower is better, but ‘lower’ isn’t the same as reaching the guideline-recommended goal for your unique risk factors,” she says.

What are the Guideline-Recommended Goals?The 2026 ACC/AHA/Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia recommends specific LDL-C goals based on individual risk. For example, below 70 mg/dL for people with diabetes and multiple cardiovascular risk factors, and below 55 mg/dL for those with cardiovascular disease at very high risk.7,*

“Knowing your LDL-C number—and talking with your doctor about what’s right for you—is one of the first steps toward understanding your risk level,” Dr. Vadali adds.

She’s also quick to retire a persistent myth. “For a lot of people, especially those already at increased cardiovascular risk, diet and exercise alone may not be enough to get LDL-C to the guideline-recommended goal,” Dr. Vadali says. “That’s not a personal failing. It’s biology. Sometimes the body needs additional help, and that’s worth a conversation with your doctor.”

For Nancy, that additional help became part of her plan. Working with her cardiologist, she started treatment with REPATHA® (evolocumab) to help lower her LDL-C and reduce her risk of a major cardiovascular event.

Repatha® is an injectable prescription medicine used:

Please see additional Important Safety Information below and full Prescribing Information.

These days, treatment is a welcome part of Nancy’s routine. “Every two weeks, I give myself an injection and have built a small ritual around it as part of my treatment plan to help keep my LDL-C at the goal my doctor recommended,” she says. “I can take it in the comfort of my own home or on the go† which is a treatment that can fit into my routine.”

Nancy is careful to say her path is her own. “I’m sharing my experience as a patient, but everyone’s situation is different,” she says. “What mattered was working with my doctor to figure out what was right for me. That’s what I want for every woman reading this to consider.”

Dr. Vadali says REPATHA is a treatment she has consistently recommended for appropriate patients. “I prescribe REPATHA because we know it starts working quickly,” she says. “For high-risk patients, keeping LDL-C lower will help reduce their risk of a life-altering event like a heart attack or stroke.”

If one thread runs through Nancy’s story, it’s the one so many women will recognize: the tendency to take care of everyone else first. “Women wear a lot of hats, and most of them involve caring for other people,” she says. “We don’t always stop to care for ourselves.”

That’s the habit she’s determined to break—in herself, and in the women who’ve heard important health messages from her for years. Her message today isn’t fear; it’s agency. “I want women to proactively understand their cardiovascular risk before something forces them to,” she says. “Ask the question: What’s my risk, and what can I do about it?”

Nancy’s ask is simple: Talk to your healthcare provider about your LDL-C and your personal cardiovascular risk factors. Get your LDL-C tested, know your doctor-recommended LDL-C goal and—if needed—make a plan with your doctor to help you reach it.

“This is the health story I never expected to tell,” Nancy says. “But if telling it means one more woman picks up the phone and calls her doctor, then it’s the most important one I’ve ever shared.”

#4936. There’s No Irony in The Armored League. Only Steel.

Welcome to NYC’s extremely violent, surprisingly wholesome new combat scene.

“THERE’S A LOT more work to do,” Damion DiGrazia muses, as 30 or so individuals spread themselves out across the gymnasium at the Manhattanville Community Center in Harlem. A pair of double doors swings lazily back and forth, marking a procession of students and the boxes they carry. DiGrazia leans against the wall, dressed in a red polo and khaki trousers, watching his small community unpack and ready itself for training.

The class does not have a format in the traditional sense. There is no lantern-jawed instructor with a whistle and a clipboard. No snap of uniforms in sync with the rhythm of a kata. There is not even, as far as I could tell, a formal warm-up. Instead, the room seems to have its own sense of internal order.

A group forms around the pieces of armor to begin the painstaking process of polishing and assessing each one for damage or repairs. Some—a breastplate, maybe a set of greaves—are singled out and ferried to a corner, where three individuals sit, cross-legged, and carefully hammer out the dents.

Ropes are thrown over the basketball hoops, and as soon as they land, students appear and begin practicing striking drills with blunted steel weapons. There are, admittedly, a lot of people with weapons. It’s a little surreal at first. When you encounter a fighter in full armor with a sword and buckler or a mace, there is a sense of visual cohesion. It is an entirely different matter to pass a fighter in cutoff denim and a T-shirt practicing elegant, sweeping strikes with an axe.

At the back of the room, the mats find their way into a rectangle, and small scrimmages begin with foam swords and shields. The training takes on its own rhythm; newer members train with foam swords and shields around the edges of the room, while the more seasoned fighters, now sporting what appear to be hockey helmets with face masks, begin grappling practice at its center. Everyone seems to know where they need to be and what they need to do.

It’s taken a long time to get here—years, actually, 13 of them, to be precise. After serving in the military, DiGrazia traces a path through Columbia University, then Harvard, before landing a job at Morgan Stanley. Finding the rhythm of corporate life increasingly dull, he sought relief through extreme sports. DiGrazia started with the classics: marathons, ultramarathons, scuba diving, skydiving, martial arts. But nothing really stuck; he was always chasing something else. That is, until a happy accident. DiGrazia tried what he thought was going to be “full-contact” LARPing (live-action role-playing), but found the experience less than fulfilling: “You couldn't punch people, couldn't grapple people, couldn't kick people, nothing,” DiGrazia says. The participants were wearing plastic armor, and a hit to the leg saw fighters taking a theatrical knee and swiping at their opponents. At the end of the practice, however, DiGrazia found himself sticking around, commiserating with another fighter, Zorikh, whom he credits as starting his journey along a path that would lead to him founding Gladiators NYC, and laying the groundwork for The Armored League.

Modern armored combat has a longer history in Europe, and DiGrazia found himself bouncing all over the continent, fighting in Poland or next to a castle in Spain. If you wanted to fight in armor, Eastern Europe was where you had to go. Stateside, the early days were decidedly underground and homebrew. Your options were more limited: small groups of fighters met in parking lots and cornfields. Orlando Mendez, one of the founding members of Gladiators NYC, remembers “a lot of horse arenas.” They were one of the few places you could throw someone into a wall without complaint. It was a sport that grew anywhere it could find space. Jason Puerta, owner of Golden Ring Combat, a West Coast armored combat group, recalls regularly fighting on the lawns of a corporate campus after securing the bemused blessing of the local security outfit. It wasn’t quite Fight Club—new members were always welcome (and still are), and people were encouraged to talk about it. Instead, the group could be said to be self-selective: “You either got the hang of it, or you just turned in your armor at the end of the day,” DiGrazia recalls. There were few rules, no weight divisions, and no weapon classes.

In these early years, the attrition rate was high. DiGrazia estimates about half of the participants quit within weeks. Even when he first secured the community center and started spreading the word about classes, he remembers sitting on a bench in the gym, staring at the doors, waiting for someone, anyone, to come to a class. Eventually, they did.

The free classes, access to equipment, loaner armor, and the open exhibition matches in New York’s Central Park—all of these, he believes, must remain core elements of the community and the sport. Gladiators NYC also has a nonprofit arm called “Santa’s Knights” where armored knights go door to door during the holidays and deliver presents to children. His commitment to this approach has not come without difficulties. DiGrazia once partnered with a martial arts school whose owner forbade him from sponsoring students who could not afford the $30 class fee. That school closed during COVID.

Technically, the sport can trace its roots back to the 14th century, when knights, foot soldiers, and men-at-arms would practice combat using dull steel weapons and a mixture of soft and plate armor. It was a way to hone their skills in times of peace. The fundamentals of the practice remain in a number of combat sports to this day, but one need only watch a bout of Olympic fencing (or “pointy tag” as Mendez described it) to realize the distance traveled. The Armored League, however, doesn’t seek a return to its medieval origins or even to the stringently historically accurate expressions, which tend to dominate in Europe. When pressed about this, DiGrazia gives an exasperated sigh: “I don't want some librarian walking around looking with a fucking magnifying glass on everybody's goddamn rivet. Leave us alone. Let's have a good time.” The aim is to bring the spectacle and joy to new audiences.

Even if, at first, you cannot follow the scoring, the fights are pure melodrama. Like any combat sport, the fighters’ stats are announced as they enter the ring—with one key distinction: their weight includes their suit of armor. Short of a quirk, it communicates the impact of the sport in a more visceral way: when a pair of combatants crash to the ground or bounce off the chain-link fencing, that’s close to 600 pounds of flesh and steel set in ballistic motion.

Bouts are divided into three to five one-minute rounds. Points are awarded based on strikes—where they land and how hard. Basic, clean strikes with weapons, shields, or fists get a base number of points. Meanwhile headshots, two-handed weapon strikes, and slugging a downed opponent get you even more. The bouts are judged by a panel set to one side of the ring, while a pair of counters runs frantically around the perimeter counting strikes.

There are comparatively few rules beyond some basic safety precautions: no stabbing or thrusting; no stomping; no strikes at the inner elbows, armpits, or the backs of knees; no slashing at the neck; and no submissions. Save for these, anything goes, and this adds to the thrill of the fights. Fighters are also not limited to their weapons, and in some cases, they will stand and trade blows like boxers. Though all of the serious fighters have broad and varied martial arts backgrounds—and training approaches—there's a roughly consistent path that leads to The Armored League. Snatches of Muay Thai knee strikes, judo sweeps, classical boxing, escrima, and BJJ are all visible in the blur of limbs, steel, and weapons. One can only imagine how the “librarians” would feel about that.

Strikes may come in flurries or great arcs, but most are hard enough to send sparks flying off the helmets. There is a marshal in the ring with the fighters, notably unarmored save for a yellow flag that’s mainly used to break the fighters up at the end of each round, which frequently ends in a tangle of armor and weapons on the floor of the ring.

There are two elements that, despite the passage of centuries, have not changed: cost and danger. Historians are divided on the exact conversion rate between 1400 and today, and most put it in terms of wages. They quote the cost of a full set of armor at somewhere between 12 and 18 months of pay. What’s universally agreed upon is that arms and armor were (and remain) anything but cheap. A full suit—then, as now—weighs anywhere from 60 to 80 pounds.

This century, prices start at around $5,000 and climb precipitously with customization. It can take anywhere from a few weeks to a year for delivery. Most participants build their suits over time as they are drawn deeper into the sport.

Building a full set is not easy. A cursory search online will lead you to a number of pages, which might appear to offer armor, but these sites are largely focused on cosplayers or LARPers. That armor will certainly hold together for a walk through Comic-Con, but it will do little to protect from a real blow. The handful of armorers still working today have long wait lists. Puerta notes that despite this, the communal nature of the sport means that much of the armor is passed down or traded between the combatants: as someone upgrades or hangs up their helmet, the armor finds its way into a new pair of hands or onto a new person’s shoulders. At Gladiators NYC, fighters who graduate from the classes, from “softs” (padded armor), and wish to try their hand at the real thing, can borrow pieces from Gladiators NYC’s own armory.

Amongst the current fighters who regularly participate in Armored League matches, almost all fight in custom armor. The suits must adhere to certain safety standards—thickness of steel, comprehensive eye protection, etc. But beyond that, there’s ample room for self-expression.

For example, Abeid “Mando” Mitchell fights in comparatively minimalist and lightweight armor and is readily recognizable by his distinctive helmet, which was made in the style of the Mandalorian from Star Wars. Luke “The Red Knight of Brooklyn” has assembled what he refers to as “a sporting replica” of 1480s armor in keeping with his own, more classical concerns.

Despite the care and attention each fighter devotes to their own armor, at all of the matches I attended, I saw weapons traded freely, shields swapped, even gauntlets lent. For as much violence as there is inside of a 60-second round, there is an equal, if not greater, level of care at the bell. The armor is not just for show; it’s for safety. Combatants want to win as much as they want to ensure their opponent walks off the field under their own power. It’s a fine balance, and as Mendez put it, “once you put on the armor and you get your ass beat a couple of times,” everybody is basically friends.

Nevertheless, it takes a toll. Puerta told me a story of how he almost lost his left eye when the tip of a sword slipped through the bars of his helmet. Others relayed stories of being crushed in a melee and of “helmet terrors” where breathing heavily in the confines of a helmet causes a buildup of carbon dioxide and creates a sensation similar to drowning.

What does the future look like? In my time with the League and Gladiators NYC, I sensed I was watching a sport in its adolescence. It is a league and community that seems to blink in the stark light of its own success and rapidly growing audience. Social media has made it easier for these once disparate communities to connect; the cornfields and horse rinks have been parlayed into an Octagon at the Melrose Ballroom in Queens or a showcase at a theater in Times Square. The bleachers that once held a smattering of friends and family have shifted into crowds drawn from all walks of life—at the sold-out show in Queens, the lines stretched around the block and some people waited an hour just to get into the venue. The Central Park exhibition matches, which happen every second Saturday of the month, have begun to draw crowds that can number over a thousand.

DiGrazia and his merry band have come a long way from the leaner years, when they struggled to find space to practice, the years when they fought in the parking lots of regional hotels in the Midwest or in the summer heat on the boardwalk in Coney Island.

Still, there is, for now, little to no money in this sport. The community, and the fighters too, all have day jobs. They are PhD students, fitness instructors, photographers, and graphic designers. One manages a magic and costume shop. Again, Fight Club springs to mind, as each goes about their day job, bearing the marks of a Thursday brawl or a weekend match, one can only wonder if anyone sees a bruise sticking out of a shirt sleeve and stops to ask just where it came from.

#4934. Jenna Dewan Faced Criticism, a Partner Suspension, and a Shock Dancing with the Stars Exit. She’s Still Proud.

In an exclusive interview with Women’s Health, the actor reflects on her time in the ballroom.

Dancing with the Stars fans let out a collective gasp Tuesday night. Jenna Dewan and her partner, Val Chmerkovskiy, had earned one of the night’s top scores: 28 out of 30. They also won their dance-off against Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik, tying for second on the leaderboard with Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov. Then host Alfonso Ribeiro called Dewan’s name, eliminating her from competition.

“I had a great time, and I loved getting to share that with the world,” she said, moments after being eliminated. “All love.”

Not even 48 hours later, Jenna sat down with Women’s Health to share her story.

Jenna Dewan: Overall, it’s really been the saying, “Two things can be true at once.” There's so many different emotions, and it's kind of hard to even put into words because obviously doing a show like this is such an enormous undertaking, and it's physically, emotionally, mentally, spiritually intense. And so, when that's just finished, it's like a light switch goes off, and then you almost don't even know where you are.

I feel all kinds of things. I feel mostly proud. I feel really proud of myself, and I feel proud of the last dance we gave on the ballroom floor, and I feel obviously sad that it's over, that I don't get to give any more dances out there and create any more special pieces. So I think it's really both. I feel really proud of us, and I feel fulfilled, and I feel filled up, and I also feel sad that the journey of creating dances is over.

JD: When you are going through the show, it feels like any week could be you. The show is not necessarily a show about dance. It's not necessarily a competition about the best dancer. It's not about the best dance you give. It's so many other elements that go into it, which is great on a reality show front-end. It makes people tune in for all different kinds of reasons, but in doing that, you never know how it's going to go.

Once it started whittling down, it was the two of us. You kind of come to a place of like, “Okay, this could be our moment.” And I had a feeling—it was a tough week as far as some of the online noise, I would say, that goes with doing the show. So it definitely wasn't out of my mind that it could be a possibility.

Even before Jenna stepped onto the DWTS dance floor, viewers debated whether she belonged in the competition. How much prior dance experience a celebrity contestant can have—while still being considered a fair competitor—has long been a point of debate among viewers.

Jenna started her career as a dancer, where she toured alongside legendary performers, including Janet Jackson (she appeared in two music videos of the singer’s). In 2006, she landed her breakout role in Step Up, in which she played a classically trained ballerina. She was the host for television shows World of Dance and Flirty Dancing as well as a judge on Come Dance with Me. Many fans of DWTS cited Jenna’s impressive resume as an unfair advantage. “How is Jenna Dewan part of this? She was a professional dancer. Hello! So unfair already,” one X user wrote on the platform after the official season 35 cast announcement.

It should be noted, however, Jenna is not the first celebrity to join the show with previous dance experience—and it’s safe to say she’ll be far from the last. Stars like Heather Morris, Jordan Fisher, and Charli D’Amelio have all undergone criticism for joining the show in the past, despite having a substantial leg up among fellow contestants. Even Alfonso, the show’s current host and season 19 winner, had prior dance experience.

JD: I will say, through the history of watching the show and what I know about the show, is I've seen there be an issue with people with dance backgrounds, and that obviously there's a lot of opinions on whether we should even have people compete on the show that have dance backgrounds.

I definitely asked quite a few times, “Are you sure you guys want me on the show?” But the incredible people who do the show were really confident in expressing to me that this show had changed a lot, and that it’s not Dancing with the Stars Who Have Never Danced. They wanted a very dynamic cast with all different levels and strengths they bring to the ballroom. I knew it would be an uphill battle for me for sure, just from the patterns of the show and the loyalists of the show and how they feel. But ultimately, the gift of doing something just for myself was really intoxicating, and it won over any sort of doubts or hesitations I had.

JD: The hardest part of the show, I would say, is it really teaches you that joy and difficulty can exist together. There were so many highs of this journey, and then so many moments of frustration and negative noise and criticism that is honestly sad, because it tries to suck out the joy from the experience.

Even for myself with a dance background, it is vulnerable to put yourself out there in the ballroom every Tuesday and be like, “Hey guys, watch my dance and tell me what you think.” And then you have the whole other element of this social, online, noisy world that is almost like they're looking to tear people down, and I felt that that was an unfortunate shade to this show that didn't need to happen.

JD: Part of the journey of the show is interesting because for the first good couple weeks, you rarely see any of the other contestants, because you are really in your own rehearsal space, and you're just trying to get the dances down as fast as you can with your partner. I think it was rare seeing people in the hallways and connecting with some of the contestants. But yeah, we definitely would talk.

I think at one point Connor [Wood] made me laugh so hard because he said he had seen some of the online social negativity, and he said, “Everyone needs to go back to journaling.” I laughed so hard, because he is exactly right. At some point, we all thought it was okay to just get online and to be mean for no reason. We are real human beings that see this and feel this, and I think that that gets forgotten.

When we did the team dance, that was when we really were able to start bonding as the contestants, because we were finally together working towards one dance and in a room together. I absolutely love them, and we were all definitely talking about this and sharing our experiences with this, and how most of us at that point, I think, had taken it off our phone or turned off social media.

JD: Naturally, because of my dance background, there were really high expectations that I put on myself, and that the world was putting on me. I didn't even realize it was happening, but it was creating this feeling that I needed to let go of perfection and kind of just get comfortable being seen and just being there. I didn't need to prove anything.

I think I just realized how much of my life I spent wanting to get things right. And this experience really challenged me in that way, because what I realized is, you just can't grow if you're constantly worried about being perfect. I had to learn to be a little uncomfortable, to be critiqued again, to make some mistakes, to be vulnerable, and just let people see me in the middle of figuring something out. There's actually a lot of freedom in that, because I didn't have ballroom dance down perfectly by the time I got out there.

JD: I thought that every dance we did. I thought that during the week two jive, and it was intriguing to me that [the judges] were so critical of certain dances. However, when I look back, there was a lot of growth for me.

There was a whole element of this that was sort of discovering my strength in a new way because I have had three children, I've navigated huge life transitions, I've built a career, a family, a life, And now, I'm stepping into this show where I'm pushing myself physically, emotionally, creatively in a way that I haven't in years. So I think I just surprised myself with how strong I am, and not just physically, but emotionally.

Jenna also faced an unexpected complication when her partner, Val, was suspended for one episode of the show following a social media post he made about DWTS judge Carrie Ann Inaba. After Carrie Ann criticized his wife, fellow pro dancer Jenna Johnson, for including what she considered an illegal lift in her routine with Harry Shum Jr., Val posted, “You almost saw Fresh Prince enter the ballroom last night.” The now-deleted post was widely interpreted as a reference to the 2022 Academy Awards, when Will Smith slapped Chris Rock after making a joke about his wife, Jada Pinkett Smith.

Carrie Ann appeared to interpret the post as a threat. She shared a screenshot of a Page Six story about it on Instagram, writing, “So this is what we are doing now?”

On Oct. 17, DWTS production company BBC Studios said Val would not participate in the Oct. 20 episode. Jenna danced with pro Alan Bersten in his place.

JD: I said this, and I really mean this, that I did not foresee having as many challenges as I did that were thrown at me during my Dancing with the Stars journey. However, the challenges of it gave me an opportunity to walk my talk, and I always think that when that happens, you can go back to your true north, to what’s your intention for doing something. How do you want to show up as a human when you’re experiencing challenges? And I kept going back to my kids. When the mid-season suspension happened, and all these things were going on, I thought, “I have a real opportunity here. I can be annoyed and bitter and upset about this, or I can show up with grace and love and joy and focus on the moment.”

That particular week was about my mom and my dedication to her. And she was in town, thrilled to have this dance with me, and thrilled to experience this moment. And I thought that this is something she's going to remember. We're all going to remember my family forever. Let's focus on that, and let's not worry about all of this that's going on.

JD: I’ve seen that, and I feel like with just life in general, even outside of Dancing with the Stars, that is absolutely something that most females have experienced. I think there's been a great change in our world, but I think for years upon years upon years, women have had a fight against misogyny and inherent bias. Women at times in life are just held to a different standard than men, and I think that that is a real reflection.

We're expected to be exceptional, but also humble and confident, but not too confident, skilled, but not struggling enough to earn praise. There's all this pressure on women. It feels like sometimes if a woman is strong or capable, the expectations become that much higher. I think people are so busy expecting women to be extraordinary that we forget to celebrate them for being extraordinary.

JD: It's never too late for a new chapter in life. And I think if there was like, one thing I wanted people to take away from my whole journey, it’s that we're never finished becoming who we are, and it's never too late to choose your own passion in life and your own joy in life. There isn't some age where you stop growing and dreaming and trying new things.

#4932. Hackers Leak Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Customer Data

Hackers Leak Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Customer Data

Three of the biggest names in payments, Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Chase, disclosed that some of their customers’ data was exposed after hackers breached third-party vendors, the latest jolt in a week of tech failures that has left Americans uneasy about the systems underpinning daily life.

The data was leaked Thursday by a ransomware group, according to a report from The Wall Street Journal. Crucially, all three firms said their own networks were not breached and that no payment systems were compromised.

A Visa spokesperson said no payment data such as card numbers was affected and that the incident involved a third-party service provider in the Asia-Pacific region.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Mastercard said a “limited amount of information from a subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program” was exposed, with no impact on its payment network.

JPMorgan said attackers targeted outside service providers and likely accessed marketing data, potentially including customer names and email addresses, with no disruption to customer services.

A ransomware group calling itself n0n claimed responsibility, according to cybersecurity firm SOCRadar. None of the three companies named the breached vendor.

Earlier in the week, JPMorgan customers hit problems accessing accounts and sending payments, which the bank attributed to a software update, and the issue spread into broader complaints about other banks.

Paired with the FAA temporarily grounding flights and an earlier Microsoft outage that locked people out of email, the week stoked unusual public anxiety about the fragility of critical tech. JPMorgan was explicit that the data leak had “no connection” to the earlier service disruptions.

For crypto users, the breach lands squarely within a growing danger that customer data, not just funds, is the soft underbelly of finance.

AI has supercharged both the scale and sophistication of cyberattacks, and 2026 has brought a steady drumbeat of data exposures. The record $6.3 billion Binance hack, tied to North Korea, laid bare how aggressively state and criminal actors are targeting financial infrastructure, while a wave of breaches has hit crypto firms through third-party vendors, echoing the vendor weakness at the center of this latest incident.

The payments giants have all leaned deeper into crypto and stablecoins this year, from Visa and Mastercard’s settlement programs to JPMorgan’s growing digital-asset footprint, making their security posture increasingly relevant to the onchain economy they’re racing to join.

For now, the firms say the damage is contained, but the episode adds to a mounting sense that no institution, however large, is immune.

#4928. The Man With No Butt

My flat ass has haunted me since high school. So I did what any man would do and sought out some wisdom from the Internet. This is the story of my midlife butt crisis.

I REMEMBER THE first time I became aware of it. Or should I say lack of it.

I grew up in the mid '80s. A magical time. MTV actually played music videos. New Coke was a thing people cared about. And a ginger-headed German teenager named Boris Becker—Boom-Boom, to his millions of fans—became, at age 17, the youngest player ever to win Wimbledon.

While other kids my age were collecting Garbage Pail Kids cards or trying to solve Rubik’s Cubes, I was rewatching VHS recordings of Becker’s matches. I practiced his signature serve motion in front of my bedroom mirror. I begged—actually begged—my parents for the complete Boris Becker starter kit: the Ellesse tennis outfit, the Puma half-top sneakers, and the holy grail itself: the Puma Super tennis racket.

The problem was, no matter how hard I tried, no matter how much Hi-C I consumed, I could never quite achieve the same explosive spring that made Boom-Boom so spectacular. Then I noticed something about Becker’s serve—the one that earned him his nickname. Most players bent their knees to generate power. Becker did something else.

He stuck out his butt. Like, really stuck it out. His serve motion involved this pronounced posterior thrust that helped him achieve that devastating topspin and pace.

I went to the bedroom mirror. Turned sideways. Attempted the same motion. And that’s when it hit me with all the force of one of Becker’s 130-mph serves: I didn’t have a butt to stick out. Where Becker had curvature, I had...continuity. My back just sort of continued into my legs.

Reality set in. No bum-bum, no boom-boom.

By high school, I had pivoted to more cerebral pursuits like creative writing and a burgeoning interest in art history. Art history seemed safe—just looking at old paintings and Roman sculptures, right? Wrong. It became immediately clear that every civilization in human history had one thing in common: great asses.

One fateful morning during my sophomore year, I was standing at my locker wearing a pair of saggy-bottomed Gap khakis when I heard giggles behind me. The distinctive sound of teenage girls discovering something hilarious and vaguely cruel.

“He has no butt!” another voice announced with the confidence of a scientist making a groundbreaking discovery. More giggling. Then came the death blow that would echo through the halls of my high school for the next two and a half years:

Sure, it wasn’t the most creative nickname, but it had just enough alliteration to spread like a pre-internet meme. From that day on, I knew “they” knew.

I RECENTLY TURNED 50. I’m happily married and have two amazing kids. Life is good, but I’d be lying if I said the ghost of No-Butt Bender doesn’t haunt me. As I’ve aged, what little I had has somehow continued to erode. My wife loves me despite my anatomical deficiency but remains perpetually baffled by the lack of rear topography. And what was once giggles from teenage girls is now full-throated hysterical laughter from my 13- and 11-year-old children when they catch a glimpse of me in anything form-fitting.

Recently, Instagram’s insecurity algorithm served me up an ad for Perk men’s clothing. Their website is a gallery of flattering middle-aged bum-shots, but what really stopped my scroll was the pitch for their pants: “Our chinos magically turn even a flat butt into a compliment magnet. Whether you’re 25 or 65, that never gets old!”

You have to understand—when you have no butt, no pants are flattering. So when Perk starts advertising pants that promise to be so bootylicious you’ll receive compliments everywhere you go, I dared to dream. I did what any man starved for posterior validation does—panic-ordered chinos in every damn color.

The moment the package arrived, I tore it open. I slipped them on, turned toward the mirror, and—holy hell—was that…something? An actual curve? A protrusion? I squinted. I turned. And I practically sprinted to the living room where the family was waiting and struck a pose.

Crickets. Then a full collapse into hysterical laughter.

“I’m sorry,” my wife gasped between laughs, “but those pants are working so hard and getting nowhere.”

I was tired of feeling like the only person other than Hank Hill to be cursed with diminished gluteal syndrome (DGS). It’s a very isolating condition. But I figured if Perk could build an entire company around flat-figured men, there had to be others out there, living their lives in quiet resignation.

Close to midnight on a Wednesday, my face lit only by the glow of my computer, I did the obvious: Googled “men with no butts.”

The search results led me to a Reddit post titled, “Gentlemen, how do you live with having no butt?” This guy laid it all out: approaching 29, finally accepting his glute-free reality, enduring constant jokes from his girlfriend, the whole nine yards of tush-less trauma. But what really got me was his closing line: “Please help.”

I stared at those two words. They contained decades of my own experience—the loneliness, the confusion, the desperation. This post was five years old, but I didn’t care. I had to reach out.

I woke the following morning to find his response waiting like a message from a long-lost brother: “You seem legit I guess. Sure why not.” We were already bonding!

I asked Ross (names have been changed to protect the in-ass-cent) what motivated him to publicly post about his crisis on Reddit, and he said, “It was a genuine problem and if someone’s got an answer that helps, I was going to be all ears.”

Ross first became aware of his DGS when a friend at the gym dropped the bomb: “Dude, you have no ass whatsoever.” The keen observation sent Ross into a spiral of photographic evidence review. He started examining pictures of himself and came to the only possible conclusion: “Huh, I guess I don’t.” It was his own bedroom-mirror moment.

As for the wisdom he received from the Reddit hivemind, he said it was mostly people prescribing the usual suspects: sprints and squats: “I was doing a shit ton of those back then and still do,” he told me. Five years later, he reports modest gains: “It’s no dump truck but I’ve got a little bit of cushion for comfort back there.” He eventually broke up with the ass-teaser (good riddance) and has been dating a new lady who actually pinches it every now and then—a gesture that, for men like us, feels like winning the Mega Millions.

But the struggle continues. Despite his Stairmaster devotion, sweatpants still “kind of sag” making it look like he may have taken a small dump in them. Still, Ross gave me the faintest glimmer that improvement was possible. Maybe a guy with no butt could transform it into a bona fide ba-donk-a-donk.

I phoned two lifelines from my past—Jonathan Botts, MD, a college friend who’d become an orthopedic surgeon at the Los Angeles Orthopedic Institute in Sherman Oaks, California, and Derek DeGrazio, Britney Spears’s former physical trainer, who had whipped me into the best shape of my life for my long-ago wedding and now is a partner at Barry’s Bootcamp Miami.

Dr. Botts (who inexplicably escaped high school without a single butt-related nickname) broke down the anatomy: the butt consists of three muscles—the gluteus maximus, medius, and minimus—but it’s the maximus that does the heavy lifting in filling out a man’s pants.

When I asked about the possibility of maximizing my non-existus, he didn’t sugarcoat it. “Here’s the problem: You can’t go from what you are now to just working on your butt and developing a huge butt,” he told me. “People are doing lots of protein intake and protein shakes and bulking up like that. You could get bigger and your butt would get bigger with you. Muscularly. But I don’t know. I don’t think you could take huge leaps with just doing squats and lunges.”

So basically, I’d need to become the Hulk to grow a butt.

Derek offered an alternate strategy with what he calls the Bender Big Three™. “I can’t say for certain, but I think No-Butt Bender can become Mild-Butt Bender with squats for foundation, Romanian deadlifts to pop your glute a little bit, and a nice hip thrust,” he said.

Mild-Butt Bender. It did have a certain je ne sais quoi.

Derek, who freely admits he was born with “a great Italian ass,” is my gluteal bizarro from an alternate universe where only perfect butts exist. He told me his seat meat gave him confidence in high school, something I could only imagine by taping Springsteen’s Born in the USA album cover to the back of my pants. Derek played baseball, a sport notorious for its revealing tight pants. “I don’t know if they came to watch baseball or if they came to watch us in our uniforms,” he recalled, misty-eyed.

I hated him. I loved him. I wanted to be him.

But then—plot twist!—just as I began fantasizing about playing shortstop, Derek dropped a bomb: “I started to realize that what was a blessing at one point became also my Achilles heel at the same time. If there is a downside, I wasn’t the fastest guy on the team.”

Wait. There was a downside to having a butt?

Dr. Botts, who describes his own posterior as “bigger than average,” delivered the final revelation: Having a bigger butt doesn’t automatically mean you have a stronger butt. “If you have a small butt, does that mean you have weak glutes? It doesn’t at all. You can have a big butt and have really weak glutes.”

All these years, I’d associated my small butt with weakness. With inadequacy. With being less than. What if I was wrong? What if, beneath my perpetually drooping pants lurked a superhero-strength posterior more powerful than even Derek’s celebrated Italian ass?

Unlikely. And who am I kidding? It’s not like if I had said to those girls in high school, “Oh no, you don’t understand—it’s really strong!” they would have stopped laughing and made out with me.

But hey, this new knowledge gives me something to cling on to. Wish I could say the same for my pants. Still, I am what I am. I am No-Butt Bender. And if that makes my kids laugh and my wife give me a warm, “It’s okay. I love you anyway” hug, I’ll take it.

#4926. Meet SHRINCS: Bitcoin's Emerging Frontrunner for a Post-Quantum Signature

Meet SHRINCS: Bitcoin's Emerging Frontrunner for a Post-Quantum Signature

Blockstream Research Director Jonas Nick, with Mikhail Kudinov and collaborators, published a security analysis on Thursday for SHRINCS, advancing an emerging frontrunner for a post-quantum signature scheme in Bitcoin.

“We need all the possible feedback—engineers, cryptographers, protocol developers,” Kudinov, a post-quantum cryptography researcher at Blockstream, said in reference to a draft of SHRINCS’ Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP). “There are a lot of things to check, test, complain about, or praise."

Notably, SHRINCS is a hash-based signature scheme that leverages SHA-256 to anchor its security in battle-tested primitives that are already used by Bitcoin, representing a conservative effort to minimize the proposal’s trust assumptions.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

That said, the scheme comes with trade-offs, most notably by introducing potential security vulnerabilities at the implementation level if misused. The scheme combines two spending paths: a small, more efficient stateful signature option and a larger, more costly stateless path with fewer security risks on the implementation side.

Although stateful signatures are compact, preserving Bitcoin’s ability to process transactions efficiently, a user can trigger a critical failure—where an attacker can forge a signature for that address and steal funds if a one-time state is accidentally reused. Because SHRINCS’ stateful path relies on one-time keys that can only safely sign a single transaction, wallet developers must carefully track each key’s state.

“It needs to be impossible for the user to behave in a way that this catastrophic event happens,” Nick told Head of MARA Foundation Isabel Foxen Duke during a recent appearance on MARA Foundation TV. “Wallet developers need to deal with this stateful component correctly.”

According to Nick, for SHRINCS to work safely in the real world, its specification and corresponding wallet implementations must automatically enforce the stateless path fallback in any situation where a state counter could possibly be compromised.

While some users might gravitate toward stateless signatures out of caution, Nick warns that widespread adoption could bloat the blockchain and drive up fees across the network.

Bitcoin’s current ECDSA signatures are typically 71 bytes long (and Taproot Schnorr signatures are 64 bytes). Under SHRINCS, stateful signatures are anywhere from 548 to 4,619 bytes, while stateless ones are 5,777 bytes. That said, optimizations of both signature paths have been accelerating with the support of AI-based research, Nick noted.

“We don’t know what the fee market will look like once we have these very big signatures,” he said. “And it’s not just the fee market, it’s also just fewer transactions fit into a block, meaning fewer people can use Bitcoin. And I think this changes the value proposition of Bitcoin.”

As the SHRINCS working group—which includes researchers backed by nonprofits including Brink and OpenSats—continues to refine the proposal’s specification, Blockstream researchers stress that getting the cryptographic foundation right is only half the battle.

Whether the broader Bitcoin ecosystem is ready to embrace SHRINCS’ inherent trade-offs will depend heavily on feedback from the network’s stakeholders in the months ahead. Meanwhile, Nick and Kudinov are requesting review of the proposal and the security analysis.

André Beganski is a Senior Content Manager at MARA Foundation, producing content on topics including the intersection of quantum computing and cryptography. He has previously worked for Decrypt.

#4925. The Best Barbour Jacket Alternatives, According to Fashion Editors

You don’t need a designer price tag to pull off one of menswear’s most iconic outerwear styles.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

I’M A SUCKER for a good Barbour jacket. I’ve always considered the British heritage brand’s waxed-cotton outerwear the perfect finishing touch to a nicely put-together fall-winter outfit. Founded in 1894, Barbour originally made weather-resistant jackets for sailors, fishermen, and outdoor workers before becoming a staple of British countryside dressing. Over the years, its association with the royal family, including Princess Diana and King Charles III, helped give the rugged outerwear an upper-class appeal. But in the past five years, Barbour has seen a major resurgence, thanks to the barn-jacket boom on runways at Prada, Loewe, and Bottega Veneta, along with a growing appetite for timeless pieces over fast fashion. Buzzy collaborations with designers like Gucci and Paul Smith, plus the popularity of British countryside style in shows like The Crown, have also introduced the look to a whole new generation of guys.

But as much as I love Barbour jackets, dropping several hundred dollars on one isn’t exactly in everyone’s budget. Some of the brand’s most iconic styles, including the Bedale, Beaufort, and Ashby, will set you back anywhere from $415 to $450. And that’s before you dive into the designer collabs. Take the latest J.Crew x Barbour Beaufort jacket. It’s a fresh, reimagined take on the brand’s signature outerwear, dressed in a bold apple-green shade with a weather-resistant finish and tartan lining. Personally, it has me in a chokehold. At nearly $500, it’s a pretty steep investment, especially if you’re just looking to dip your toes into the barn-jacket trend.

Thankfully, you don’t have to spend that kind of money to capture the same British countryside charm. Plenty of menswear brands have put their own spin on the classic barn jacket, offering similar silhouettes, canvas fabrics, and utilitarian details at more digestible prices. I’ve rounded up some stylish Barbour jacket alternatives from brands like Bonobos and Quince that look just as sharp, whether you’re getting dressed up or keeping it casual.

Of all the Barbour jacket alternatives I’ve tested, Quince’s version comes close in comparison to the Barbour x Paul Smith collaboration I already own. That jacket runs north of $800, while Quince’s costs just over a hundred bucks but with nearly all the same bells and whistles: a two-tone brown colorway, contrasting corduroy collar, and snap-button storm throat flap that helps seal out drafts of wind. There’s also a two-way zipper that lets me open the jacket from the bottom when I need a little more breathing room.

It’s made from 100% organic cotton and fully lined with soft cotton flannel, which adds a welcome layer of warmth on chilly days when I can skip wearing a bulky sweater underneath. The cut hits just below the waist, with a roomy fit that leaves plenty of space for layering without feeling overly baggy. I’ve even worn it through a few light rain showers, and the fabric didn’t get soaked. I also appreciate how the classic design makes it easy to dress up with trousers and an Oxford shirt or keep things casual with jeans and boots.

Uniqlo makes one of the best affordable Barbour alternatives I’ve come across, and at just $80, it looks and feels more expensive than it actually is. The lightly padded cotton-nylon fabric provides just enough warmth for temps below 60 degrees. What I especially like is the clean, sleek design that comes with a concealed front closure that hides the buttons and zipper, giving the jacket a sharper, more polished look when fully fastened. There’s also a classic checked lining and two-way flap pockets that can be accessed from the top or sides.

Fit-wise, it has a relaxed, boxy silhouette that hits right at the waist and leaves enough room to comfortably layer a chunky knit over a dress shirt. And unlike some barn jackets that lean heavily into the rugged workwear aesthetic, this one feels a little more understated. It comes in versatile neutrals like olive, khaki, black, and dark brown, so finding one that works with your wardrobe shouldn’t be difficult.

If you’re looking for something that puts a slightly different spin on the traditional barn jacket, Bonobos has you covered. Its Canvas Ranch Jacket trades the usual waxed-cotton construction for a sturdy cotton-elastane blend that has a little stretch, so I’m not feeling boxed in. But what really caught my attention are the angled patch pockets across the front. They’re a subtle departure from the usual straight-cut or flap pockets you see on most field jackets, giving the whole design a more distinctive, modern feel.

The cut extends past the waist and lands around the upper thigh, offering a little more coverage than your typical trucker jacket. I also like that Bonobos keeps the color options simple with midnight navy and forest green, both of which go nicely with denim, chinos, or tailored trousers.

For guys who want the classic Barbour look with a little more protection against the elements, consider this insulated version from L.L.Bean. Unlike some of the lighter options on this list, this one is packed with 60 grams of PrimaLoft Black insulation, a lightweight synthetic fill that helps keep it toasty inside without the bulk of a heavy winter coat. The 100% cotton exterior has a water-resistant waxed finish that will keep you dry in light rain. It also has a quilted exterior that gives the traditional field-jacket silhouette a slightly more outdoorsy vibe.

It’s slightly fitted, so guys who are super jacked might have to size up. But the regular-length cut makes it easy to wear over everyday layers and not feel overly snug. This is a great option for construction laborers, landscapers, and other guys who spend long hours outdoors. It’s more practical than fashion-forward, but you get the timeless look of a heritage field jacket with added insulation and weather protection that make it useful beyond just completing an outfit.

Flint and Tinder’s waxed trucker jacket famously appeared on Pedro Pascal in HBO’s The Last of Us, and we’ve been major fans ever since. This is a burly, no-nonsense trucker jacket made from Martexin waxed sailcloth that’s treated on both sides to help block wind and repel light rain. The antique-finish metal buttons and earthy color options give it that rugged, worn-in look that only gets better with age. On the inside, a full-length blanket-style lining keeps you cozy during 50-degree mornings.

One thing worth mentioning is that the waxed fabric feels pretty stiff at first, so don’t expect it to have that soft, broken-in feel right out of the gate. But that’s also part of the appeal of this type of outerwear. After three wears, the fabric gradually softens and develops more character. Compared to Barbour’s longer field jackets, this one has a more traditional trucker silhouette, so I can pair it with jeans, boots, and other casual staples.

Not every Barbour alternative needs to look like it belongs in the English countryside. Case in point: AYR’s The Club, which takes a more refined approach. It’s made from stonewashed cotton-hemp denim that gives it a softer, lived-in look. The fabric is also light enough to wear across three seasons, making it a versatile option for those in-between days when a heavy coat feels like overkill.

I can throw it over a tee with jeans for the weekend or wear it with a collared shirt and trousers to the office. Just keep in mind that this isn’t the jacket I’d wear in the rain, since the fabric isn’t designed to repel water like traditional waxed cotton. And at a little over $300, it’s certainly not the cheapest alternative on this list. Still, if you’re after something that feels more stylish than rugged, this one makes a strong case for itself.

#4924. This Common Drug Was Just Linked to a 24% Lower Risk of Dementia

For all of the havoc dementia causes to a person's life, scientists are still trying to figure out exactly how to prevent it. While keeping your brain and body active and following a healthy diet seems to help, there doesn't seem to be a pill you can pop to lower your risk of developing the devastating disease. But new research suggests that a common osteoporosis drug might be worth investigating further.

It's a class of medications called nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (or NBPs). While these are typically used to strengthen bones in people with osteoporosis, NBPs could have the added benefit of supporting brain health as you age, too.

It's important to stress this now: The researchers found a link between people who used NBPs and a lower risk of dementia, but they didn't prove that the medications themselves actually dropped the risk. Still, doctors say there could be something to this. "The association is intriguing," says Anna Hohler, MD, director of neurology for Northwell Health's Westchester Region, and chair of neurology at Phelps Hospital and Northern Westchester Hospital.

Here's what experts want you to take away from the findings.

Meet the experts: Ching-Lung Cheung, PhD, study co-author and associate professor in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at the University of Hong Kong; Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John's Health Center in Santa Monica, California; and Anna Hohler, MD, director of neurology for Northwell Health's Westchester Region, and chair of neurology at Phelps Hospital and Northern Westchester Hospital.

The study, which was published in the journal Alzheimer's & Dementia, analyzed the electronic medical records of more than 120,000 patients aged 60 and older in Hong Kong. All of the participants had osteoporosis or fractures due to fragility (meaning, their bones had weakened).

Researchers discovered that people who took NBPs had a 16 percent lower risk of developing Alzheimer's disease and related dementias compared to those who didn't take medication for osteoporosis. But when they compared those who used NBPs to those taking other types of osteoporosis medications, the dementia risk was 24 percent lower.

The link seemed to be especially strong in women and patients who had hip fractures.

The researchers were inspired to look into NBPs and Alzheimer’s because the drug had been shown to improve cognitive function in previous animal models of neurotoxicity and Alzheimer’s disease, says Ching-Lung Cheung, PhD, study co-author and associate professor in the Department of Pharmacology and Pharmacy at the University of Hong Kong. “These findings led us to investigate whether their use might also be associated with a lower risk of dementia in humans."

While the study didn't prove that NBPs were responsible for the lowered risk, doctors have a few theories on what could be driving this.

For one, it’s possible that the link is more indirect, according to Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John's Health Center in Santa Monica, California. NBPs improve bone density over time, which allows people to be more active, Dr. Segil says. "Broken bones do not cause dementia but do decrease activity," he says. (Being sedentary is a risk factor for dementia.)

There may also be something about NBPs themselves that could lower the risk of dementia, though. "Some researchers speculate that these medications could influence inflammation, immune pathways, or other biological processes involved in neurodegeneration," Dr. Hoehler says. But, she points out, more research is needed.

For now, doctors don't plan to prescribe NBPs in an effort to lower dementia risk. But Dr. Cheung says it should make people feel confident about using this class of medication for bone health. "Given the low uptake of osteoporosis treatment, people with osteoporosis should consider appropriate anti-osteoporosis medication, which may offer an additional benefit for brain health," he says. Even though osteoporosis drugs are commonly available, uptake has been historically low—studies have previously estimated that around seven percent of women with osteoporosis actually take medication for it.

Ultimately, doctors say that a clinical trial is needed to see if NBPs actually lower the risk of dementia. "If future studies confirm these results, they could open an exciting new avenue for Alzheimer's prevention or treatment," Dr. Hoehler says.

#4923. ‘I Picked Up Weights for the First Time in My Mid-50s. I Was Powerlifting by My 70s—Here’s How’

“Getting stronger takes patience, consistency, and a willingness to step outside my comfort zone, but the reward is so worth it.”

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

If I’ve learned anything over the past few years, it’s to just say yes. Saying the word was simple, but ended up changing my relationship with fitness—and transforming my whole life.

I’ve always loved being physically active and moving my body; I ran track and field in high school, played field hockey in both high school and college, and enjoyed horseback riding as a young adult. But shortly after graduating, I had my first of seven children at 23. From that point on, I went straight into parenting mode: My family became my priority, and with so much to juggle, exercise took a back seat for the next few decades.

But at 55, I wanted to feel strong in my body again. My kids were grown and I had more free time, so I signed up for a gym membership. I even started working with a personal trainer to make sure I was doing the right moves safely. Over the next 15 years, I exercised with several trainers, lifting light weights once or twice a week with dumbbells and weight machines. I enjoyed the workouts and saw improvements to my overall fitness, but I wasn’t particularly passionate about going to the gym, so I wasn’t always consistent and never set any real goals.

Then, at 70, everything changed. My trainer who I had come to enjoy working with and trust moved away, and without that connection, I stopped going to the gym. But after about a year away, the fitness manager at my gym, Nate Fleming, reached out to me, and I began working with him twice a week.

He immediately changed up my programming and introduced me to the idea of progressive overload. I learned that gradually increasing the weight I lifted each week could help me build muscle, get stronger, and see real results. He also added new movements to my routine, like farmer’s carries, deadlifts, and squat variations. Deadlifts, in particular, became one of my favorite exercises—I loved that the move required so much technique. There was something so satisfying about picking up a heavy weight and realizing I could lift more than I thought.

Nearly overnight, my attitude toward fitness changed: I enjoyed being challenged and discovering how much stronger I could become when I pushed myself. Over the next year, I began to see visible muscle definition in my arms and legs and felt more energized throughout the day. More importantly, though, my confidence skyrocketed because I had developed a greater trust in my own abilities.

I had grown to love lifting heavy, and wanted to step outside my comfort zone and discover what I could accomplish in my 70s. I casually asked Nate if there were deadlifting competitions for older women, and he said there were. So, I took a leap of faith and started a seven-month training process for a powerlifting competition (which took place this past March). I upped my training to three days a week, continuing to progressively increase the weights, and worked on refining my technique to move more efficiently.

The day of the competition was one of the best days of my life. I decided to compete in all three lifts: I squatted 132 pounds, bench-pressed 71.5 pounds, and deadlifted 242 pounds, setting records in all three lifts for my age and weight category in Nova Scotia, Canada, where I live. I was so proud of what I’d accomplished and felt incredibly empowered by what my body could do at 71. My kids and grandkids were also there to cheer me on, which made the day even more special. Sharing that moment with my family and showing them what was possible at my age meant so much to me. I walked away feeling stronger, more confident, and excited to do it again.

My next powerlifting competition is this month, and I still lift with Nate three days a week. My training is structured in four-week blocks, and the weight, sets, and reps change each week. For instance, in week one, I might do 3 sets of 5 reps at a moderate weight. Then, I gradually increase the load in weeks two and three while lowering the reps as I get closer to my heaviest lifts. Week four is a deload week, so I reduce the weight and give my body a chance to recover before lifting heavier again.

Each workout starts with the main lift (deadlift, squat, or bench press) because that’s when I have the most energy. Then, I move on to three or four accessory exercises, where I use lighter weights to strengthen supporting muscles, address weaknesses, and improve my performance in the main lifts. For example, on deadlift day, I might incorporate exercises like lunges, hamstring curls, and bent-over rows to strengthen my glutes, hamstrings, and back.

I’m incredibly proud of my progress over the last six months. I have a lingering shoulder injury, so right now, my bench press has stayed about the same at 71.5 pounds. But I can squat 160 pounds and deadlift 265 pounds, which is only five pounds away from the Canadian deadlift record.

While I train hard, I recover even harder in between sessions. I get seven to eight hours of sleep each night and am mindful about nutrition, eating lots of protein, since it’s important for building and maintaining muscle. I aim for around 120 grams a day, with eggs, chicken, and fish as some of my go-to sources. Additionally, during rest days, I focus on stretching and hip and shoulder mobility to improve my range of motion. I don’t count my steps, but I try to walk as much as I can throughout the day to keep my body moving and maintain cardiovascular health.

I love Feetures socks for their snug arch support and gentle compression that keeps them comfortably in place during workouts.

Clif Builders are my favorite post-workout snack since they taste great and pack 20 g of protein per bar.

When I first decided to work with a personal trainer in my 50s, I wanted guidance, accountability, and the confidence that I was exercising safely and effectively—and I got that. My first few trainers helped me build a foundation by teaching me proper form and the fundamental movements that I still rely on today.

But working with Nate completely changed my relationship with lifting: He knows how to motivate me, pushing me without going beyond my abilities. When I attempt a new personal record, his belief in me helps me believe in myself, too. Now, I know what I’m capable of and how to challenge myself while lifting safely. The gym has become so much more than a place to work out—it’s where I keep discovering what I can do.

I’ve learned that getting stronger isn’t just about how hard I work in the gym—it’s also about how well I recover between workouts through getting plenty of sleep, mobility work, stretching, and walking. When I don’t make time for recovery activities or I don’t fuel properly, it makes a difference; I feel more fatigued, have less energy during workouts, and struggle to perform at the same level.

For me, progress doesn’t mean pushing myself to the limit every day. It means finding the right balance between challenging my body and giving it the rest and support it needs to keep getting stronger.

If you’d told me a few years ago that I’d be powerlifting in my 70s and chasing a deadlift record, I never would have believed you. Before I started training with Nate, I had never really set big fitness goals or thought about pushing my limits. But that began to change when I realized how much stronger I could become with the right coaching and encouragement. I was inspired to set goals that challenged me in new ways I never thought possible, and I’ve learned that it’s never too late to surprise myself and try something new. Having a goal to work toward keeps me motivated, and I love seeing how far I can push myself when I have the right support and plan in place.

Of course, getting stronger takes patience, consistency, and a willingness to step outside my comfort zone, but the reward is so worth it. I hope my journey encourages other women, especially those in their 60s and 70s, to keep challenging themselves and try new things. They might discover a passion they never knew they had, just as I did.
