#4922. How to Lose Your Love Handles

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

WHEN YOU THINK about a lover’s touch, your brain might jump to a pair of hands lingering around the hips—which might explain the origin of the term "love handles." It’s a cute nickname, but you’d probably describe love handles themselves as anything but cute.

The term refers to the pesky fat that sits on top of your hip bones, and lots of guys want it gone. “Many men are concerned about how to lose weight in their midsection. I let them know that their body has an android distribution, or male-like, weight distribution,” says Fatima Cody Stanford, M.D., M.P.H., obesity medicine physician and Men's Health advisor.

While there’s no way to lose fat from your midsection only without medical intervention, there are several ways to bring down your overall body fat which will pull from all areas. If losing your love handles is what will help boost your confidence and make you a healthier, happier version of yourself, that's a fine goal to have. Just remember that there's more to health than how you look, and you can set your sights on other outcomes, too (like getting stronger more generally or something like body recomposition more specifically).

LOVE HANDLES ARE what most people commonly call the bundle of subcutaneous fat that lies just above your pant line, sitting directly under the skin. That’s actually good news, because it means it’s not the dangerous kind of fat, called visceral fat, that can sit on your organs and put unnecessary (and life-threatening) pressure on them. Adipose fat, such as the love handles, can act as energy deposits. When our bodies lose other energy intake (food), we can use these deposits to power our bodily functions.

Even though our bodies have good intentions when collecting these love handles, it doesn’t mean they’re impossible to lose. But it will involve a solid calorie deficit and some effort in the gym.

There are a few shortcuts you can take, but they're extreme, and not something that we'd generally recommend. Liposuction is one of these options. More recently, men have turned to non-invasive treatments, the most popular of which feature either freezing or heating the stubborn fatty areas off the body. Some guys might also turn to using drugs like a GLP-1 (which can’t target one specific problem area), if a doctor recommends their use. These treatments are expensive and might be a bridge too far, unless you're really desperate.

Besides, by cutting corners, you'll miss out on the fitness gains you'd make along the way using other methods, which will hopefully become a reason you're training, regardless of the aesthetic payoff. If getting rid of love handles without special treatments is your goal, you'll have to work hard—and you'll have to work smart, too.

One method that is not smart and won't work is spot reduction. The theory is that if you focus all of your attention on one specific area in your training (for instance, doing hundreds of crunches for you midsection), you'll be able to burn off the fat in just that area.

But that's not how your body works. What you can do is lose fat more generally, then build up muscle where you might not have had it before—but for that to work, you'll have to do that smart, hard work. That’s also the case for GLP-1 use. If you go that route, make sure you understand how to train with a program like the MH GLP-1 Muscle Growth plan.

HERE’S A PLAN to ditch your stubborn love handles from former Men's Health fitness advisor Craig Ballantyne, C.S.C.S.

Studies have shown that interval-based exercise programs, most specifically high intensity interval training (HIIT), are more effective for burning off your love handles than steady state cardio. Instead of running for miles on end without any clear goal, fine tune your work and rest periods to strip away the fat.

So what type of interval program should you use? You can use a jump rope, or apply the principles to running or weight room work. Ballantyne recommends this setup to banish that pesky midsection fat:

After a thorough warmup, alternate between 20 seconds of hard exercise and 40 seconds recovery. Repeat that pattern 6 to 8 times. Afterwards, finish with 5 to 10 minutes of cooldown exercise.

If you have extra time, do 10 minutes of regular cardio pace.

Even though Ballantyne recommended cardio for a cool down, he's wary of its effectiveness when performed alone. Extended periods of steady state cardio, like jogging, won’t do much to cut down your spare tire. "It's not going to work as well as interval training," Ballantyne said.

This is related to another issue, according to Ballantyne: Many guys don't have enough muscle in the first place. Losing love handles, like bodybuilding, is a game of illusion. Muscle on your chest and back can essentially "hide" excess fat in your love handle area.

"So most guys are “skinny-fat,” and then try to lose love handles with cardio only, and basically become even smaller versions of themselves—but still skinny-fat," Ballantyne said. "It's better to use intervals and weight training to gain muscle and lose fat at the same time—which IS possible—and change your body's overall appearance."

"Ab exercises like crunches are generally a waste of time," Ballantyne said. The problem is, you’re only working the muscles around your lower spine with crunches and situps.

Instead, you should build up your core with moves that focus on spinal stability, like planks and hollow body holds. Check out this quick video about the way your core muscles function for an idea of what you should be aiming for:

Want a smarter core workout in general? Check out Epic Abs, the program from MH fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. that inspired this video.

While you're cutting down your midsection, do yourself a solid and work on some other areas of your body that can take attention away from your ample hips. Build up your pecs, lats, deltoids, and traps to create the illusion of smaller love handles.

"Most guys don't have enough muscle to focus on just losing weight," Ballantyne said, "so every guy must build some muscle in these areas."

How can you build the muscle and lose fat at the same time? You're hoping to "culk," so you should start by training hard, eating properly, and sticking to a consistent program.

Ballantyne also recommended a plan based around two to three total body workouts per week. Use five exercises per workout (one lower body, one upper push, one lower body single leg, one upper pulling, one total body ab exercise). Do that as a circuit three times through, with eight to 12 reps per exercise. Finish with interval training.

For best results, follow a plan that fits your unique training needs. Use our Workout Finder below to get a personalized recommendation based on your age, fitness level, and other key factors.

You can't neglect nutrition if you're looking to lose fat. After all, losing fat means burning more calories then you take in, or creating a calorie deficit. Here’s how to calculate a healthy calorie deficit based on your body and goals.

There are easy eating hacks you can incorporate into your daily routine to cut calories while still enjoying yourself and staying satisfied. Eliminating foods you love is an unsustainable way to live. "Negotiate with yourself on what you are willing to do without or do with less of," says Leslie Bonci, R.D., sports dietitian for Kansas City Chiefs.

Prioritize and optimize protein, fiber, healthy fats, and produce to fill up. Protein and fiber help you stay fuller, longer—which may reduce snacking in between meals. When choosing grains, pick the higher fiber choices like quinoa, oatmeal, and whole wheat pastas. Incorporate more beans into your salads, soups, and even blend and add to sauces. Include a fruit or a veggie at every occasion.

When it comes to snacking, focus on foods that will make you chew longer and eat slower, like jerky or apples. Bean dips with veggies are also a quick and easy snack that will load up the fiber and protein with little calories.

To really find a custom nutrition plan that will work best with your body, talk to a registered dietitian.

We don’t need to tell you that losing weight is no walk in the park. Accomplishing your goals will take a balance of overhauled nutrition, exercise, and recovery practices to complete the equation and finally shed some of those pounds. You might find it tough to do any of those things on your own.

Working with a professional can help provide some much needed accountability and guidance. Doctors who specialize in weight loss, nutritionists, dietitians, and personal trainers can all help you get to where you want to be. They can tailor your workouts and meal plans to better match your genetic makeup and goals. Don’t be afraid to ask for help if the task feels daunting.

SORRY TO BREAK it to you—doing loads of side bends and Russian twists won’t melt away your love handles. It’s impossible to lose fat on one portion of your body by exercising the muscles in that area. The concept is called spot training, or spot reduction—and it doesn’t work.

What does work is incorporating high-velocity compound movements into your workouts. Compound movements are exercises that require multiple muscle groups working together. These kinds of moves will burn a lot of calories, aiding in creating the calorie deficit you need to burn fat all over. Here are 6 of our favorites.

This move lights up your body head to toe, and ramps up your heart rate in the process. Not only will med ball slams aid in the fat loss process, but they’ll help you take a little aggression out on your worst days.

Sets and Reps: Aim for 2 to 3 sets of 30 second sets, either as a warm up or programmed into your next conditioning circuit.

The dumbbell snatch is one of the best movements for building full body power and strength. Almost your entire body has to work to power the weight up and overhead.

Sets and Reps: Aim for 3 sets of 3 to 5 reps with a heavy weight, or build it into a conditioning set by doing 30 seconds of work, 30 seconds of rest with a medium weight.

The kettlebell swing is a fundamental core exercise that works practically every muscle in your body. Be careful about ramping up the weight too quickly though—this move has a ton of subtleties that are vital to the safety of the movement.

Sets and Reps: Do 4 sets of 10 to 12 reps with a heavy weight, or build it into a conditioning set by doing 30 seconds of work, 30 seconds of rest with a medium weight.

Burpees are infamous for a reason. It looks simple, but do it the right way and you’ll feel way more of a challenge than you’d expect.

Sets and Reps: Aim 3 to 4 rounds of 20 seconds on, 40 seconds off, or build it into a conditioning circuit.

Mountain climbers are a staple core exercise that will challenge your upper body too as you maintain that high plank position.

Sets and Reps: Set a timer for 6 minutes and aim for 20 seconds of work, 10 seconds of rest for a good core burn, build it into a conditioning circuit.

This multi-joint movement combines a front squat and a push press to incorporate the whole body to build power and strength—and torch calories, too.

Sets and Reps: Aim for 3 sets of 6 to 8 reps, build it into a conditioning circuit for 30 seconds of work, 30 seconds of rest.

#4921. Why higher rates could slow Bitcoin buying at treasury firms

A treasury company can have years of dividends covered and still struggle to sell new shares on terms that make another Bitcoin purchase worthwhile.

Rising US interest rates could slow buying by Bitcoin treasury companies long before they have trouble paying their bills.

Strategy raised $244.7 million by selling common stock in the week ended Nov. 15. It spent $206.3 million of the proceeds buying back preferred shares and $33.4 million on 485 BTC.

At the time, its US dollar assets covered more than three years of preferred dividends and debt interest at current payouts. When Treasury bills pay more, investors can demand a higher yield to buy newly issued preferred shares.

For common stock, StoneX analyst Mark Palmer watches how much investors will pay above the value of the Bitcoin each share represents. At a premium, a company can issue stock and buy enough Bitcoin (BTC) to leave shareholders with more BTC per share. However, as that premium narrows, so does the gain.

#4920. Nvidia, AMD, Micron Sink as Anthropic Closes 17% Above IPO Price

Nvidia, AMD, Micron Sink as Anthropic Closes 17% Above IPO Price

Anthropic made stock market history Thursday, raising $81.34 billion in the largest initial IPO share sale ever. But Wall Street's response was considerably less enthusiastic than the demand for the Claude developer's shares.

The stock opened at $111.50 on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, a 34% premium over its $83 offering price, briefly pushing the company's fully diluted valuation past $2 trillion.

The rally faded quickly, however, with shares dropping toward $93 before closing today at $97.17.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The offering involved 980 million shares and surpassed SpaceX's original $75 billion IPO in June. As Decrypt previously reported, SpaceX's expanded final offering reached $86.25 billion, meaning Anthropic has not surpassed that completed deal.

Investors initially welcomed the listing, sending technology stocks higher before the opening bell. By the afternoon, however, the Nasdaq Composite was down 2.06%, the S&P 500 had fallen 1.9%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was off 2.17%.

The selloff extended across the AI supply chain. A Thursday afternoon market heatmap showed Nvidia falling 3.4%, Broadcom losing 2.07%, and memory chipmaker Micron slipping 2.17%. Microsoft was down 1.97%, while cloud infrastructure and software provider Oracle declined 2.97%.

AMD was among the hardest hit, down 7.73% in the day, although its decline had a separate catalyst. Reuters reported that the chipmaker came under pressure after investigative outlet Hunterbrook disclosed that its affiliated investment fund had taken a short position in the company.

The picture was not uniformly negative. Palo Alto Networks rose 6%, CrowdStrike gained 2.24%, and Intel added 2.25% in the same snapshot. The divergence shows that investors were distinguishing between companies rather than selling every technology stock indiscriminately.

The broader weakness comes as investors question the cost of building AI infrastructure and the returns companies can generate from that spending. Nvidia's latest earnings beat expectations, but uncertainty following Jensen Huang's resignation has continued to weigh on the semiconductor giant.

Anthropic also faces an expensive expansion. Its IPO disclosures detailed approximately $900.9 billion in infrastructure and computing commitments extending through 2045, alongside another $150 billion to $175 billion in estimated payments under less precisely defined arrangements.

"Anthropic's record-breaking IPO has failed to rekindle enthusiasm for tech stocks," Joe Maher, market economist at Capital Economics, told Reuters.

Nvidia's weakness was notable given its latest results. The chipmaker reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue on Tuesday, up 103% from a year earlier, and forecast stronger-than-expected sales for the following quarter.

Even those numbers failed to erase concerns over the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang after allegations of extramarital affairs and possible leaks of corporate secrets and the sustainability of the AI spending boom.

The pressure also reached companies that rent out computing capacity. Neocloud operators CoreWeave and Nebius fell 5.0% and 7.8%, respectively. Software companies were weak as well: Salesforce declined 3.17% and Adobe lost 2.03% in the afternoon heatmap. From chips and data centers to enterprise software, the losses extended beyond any single corner of the AI trade.

Anthropic's IPO prospectus shows how closely these companies are tied together. Nvidia and Google each committed roughly $10 billion to a conditional private share placement alongside the IPO.

AMD agreed to invest $2.5 billion; Broadcom, Micron and Microsoft committed $1 billion apiece; and TSMC pledged $500 million. The $26 billion placement is separate from the public offering. Several of these investors are also key suppliers or infrastructure partners in the AI ecosystem.

That creates a central question for investors: How much of the money flowing into AI companies will ultimately translate into profitable demand for chips, cloud capacity and software?

Anthropic's blockbuster debut demonstrates demand for its shares, but Thursday's broader decline shows that Wall Street is not ready to extend that confidence to every company financing or supplying the AI boom.

#4919. Mel Robbins Started Lifting Weights in Her 50s. Here’s What Her Gym Routine Looks Like

The podcast host breaks it down on the latest episode of Strong Like.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Mel Robbins has always been a mover—running, hiking, skiing, Pilates, yoga, you name it—but it’s only been recently that the 58-year-old has added strength training to her fitness regimen. She credits Dr. Stacy Sims (a Women’s Health advisory board member) and Dr. Vonda Wright, both guests on The Mel Robbins Podcast, with finally persuading her to lift weights.

“They kept saying, when we reach a certain age, 40 and up, for us to start resistance training and with heavier weights,” says Mel, who had to overcome a few fitness myths to finally prioritize pumping iron. “I was nervous I would bulk up. That's a joke, because you know how much you need to train to actually bulk up? I wasn't going to be doing that.”

So what exactly does Mel do in the gym? She walked WH through a typical session for the latest episode of Strong Like.

Before Mel’s feet ever touch a mat, she makes sure to jot down—with actual pen and paper!—what she intends to do at the gym. “This will ensure that you actually do it, because if you're relying on this noggin up here, it ain't happening,” she says.

With her to-do list by her side, Mel begins her session with a warm-up. She runs through a batter of stretches that include inchworms (with an added push-up—go Mel!) and lunges with a twist, before moving on to a banded overhead press to mobilize her shoulders. “I've stopped judging these little bands,” Mel says. “These little suckers look like nothing. Let me tell you, there's a whole lot of something in these bands. You'll be shocked at how much gain you can get and how great this is for you.”

With her warm-up complete, she moves on to the workout, shifting the bands from her arms to her legs for a duck walk. Mimicking the water fowl, she moves forward and back, side to side, keeping outward pressure on the bands.

Next, she tackles one of her favorite moves, a reverse lunge with medicine ball twist. “It's a compound movement that works mobility, your core, your arms, your legs, everything in one movement,” Mel says. “It's super-simple, painful, and awful, and it works like a charm.”

She moves on to the upper body with chest presses, though she has a hack for lighting up even more muscles in the process. “If you want to maximize what you're doing here, suck in your stomach and clench your butt, because then it's not just arms; it's a whole-body thing,” she says.

Finally, she concludes with a snatch, joking: “You can work out a lot of aggression at the world doing [these].”

Ultimately, says Mel, her approach to fitness is pretty straightforward: “I'm not in here because I want to look good in a bathing suit. I do, but that's not the motivation. I'm in here lifting weights because I want to live a long, vibrant, healthy life. I want to be dancing into my late 90s. I want to make sure I can pick up the suitcase and put it up in the overhead. I want to make sure that I am strong so my life is long.”

To hear more about Mel’s gym motivation, click play on the latest episode of Strong Like above!

The fit is generous, allowing space to pile base layers and still keep a clean profile.

Down and synthetic insulation are two of the most common options.

Synthetic insulation is made from polyester fibers, more affordable than down, and handles wet weather better. Popular options include PrimaLoft and Thinsulate, which use a blend of synthetic fibers designed to trap heat while remaining lightweight and breathable.

Down is made from clusters of goose or duck plumage, and is prized for its lightweight warmth. It compresses easily for packing and offers superior heat retention in dry conditions. Some coats even blend down and synthetic fill to combine the benefits of both.

Look for a waterproof shell, sealed seams, and a protective hood to help keep rain and snow from soaking through. Features like adjustable cuffs and storm flaps can also help block out wind and moisture. If you’re dealing with wet, snowy winters, prioritize a fully waterproof design over a water-resistant finish.

A winter coat should leave enough room to layer a sweater or hoodie without feeling bulky or restricting movement. The shoulders should sit comfortably, the sleeves should cover the wrists, and the hem should provide enough coverage for your needs. If you plan to wear it over heavier layers, consider sizing up, but always check the brand’s fit recommendations.

Look for fleece-lined hand pockets to keep your fingers warm and interior pockets to protect your phone, wallet, or AirPods from the cold. Extra details like zippered or hidden pockets add practicality, especially for commuting, travel, or outdoor adventures.

Our fashion team, led by Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, tested more than 40 winter coats in real-world conditions, from freezing city commutes to snowy hikes, ski trips, and travel days spent shuffling between cold-weather airports. If a coat claimed to handle winter, we made sure it proved it. We focused on warmth, durability, fit, mobility, and practicality. We paid attention to how each coat insulated in different temperatures, whether the materials could stand up to wind and wet weather, how well the coat moved with us during long days out, and whether the design felt useful rather than overbuilt.

Details like pocket placement, zippers, adjustability, and overall comfort played a big role too. After months of wear and side-by-side comparisons, only the top performers made our final list. These are the winter coats that stayed warm, held up, and made our lives easier—not just in theory, but in brutal winter reality.

For most of us, the terms "jacket" and "coat" are probably interchangeable. However, the main difference comes down to length and coverage. A winter coat's main objective is to keep you warm, which is why it's bigger and thicker, extends past the hips or toward the knees, and is filled with some type of insulation. A jacket, on the other hand, is considered a combination of style and warmth. Jackets don't typically go past the waist and they're designed to be worn indoors at times. Winter jackets can be layered more with outfits too—sometimes even under a coat.

Winter jackets can work as your main outer layer in cold weather, especially when they’re insulated and long enough to provide adequate coverage. For colder temperatures or extended time outdoors, a longer, more heavily insulated coat or parka can provide additional warmth and protection. The right choice ultimately depends on the weather, your activity level, and how much you plan to layer underneath.

#4917. Citi Says Customers Are Responsible When AI Banking Agents Go Rogue—Even After a Hack

Citi Says Customers Are Responsible When AI Banking Agents Go Rogue—Even After a Hack

Citi has updated its online banking terms to make customers responsible for the actions of third-party AI agents accessing their accounts, including when an agent leaks their credentials and someone else uses them to get in.

The change, reported by TechCrunch Wednesday, makes explicit how the bank intends to handle an increasingly awkward question: Who pays when software handling your money makes a mistake?

Under Citi’s new terms, actions taken using credentials supplied to an outside agent are treated as authorized by the customer, even if the tool ignores instructions, exceeds its permissions, or shares those credentials with another party.

Citi says it has no obligation to investigate whether the agent followed the customer's original prompts, subject to applicable law.

A Citi spokesperson told TechCrunch that the November revision clarifies the risks of sharing banking credentials or granting outside tools account access. The provision does not apply to AI agents offered by Citi itself.

Citi is not acting alone. JPMorgan and Bank of America announced similar policies in October, while Citizens Bank warned customers this week by email that they could be responsible for what their AI assistants do.

PNC also changed its digital agreement on Wednesday. Its rules distinguish bank-approved connections, which can provide limited access, from handing an agent unrestricted access to an account.

The move follows a banking security scare from October 22. Major banks had detected AI agents logging into customer accounts, sometimes taking steps that appeared to go beyond their users' instructions, and executives said they struggled to determine which agents had been properly authorized.

An AI agent differs from a conventional chatbot because it can act on a user's behalf, potentially navigating websites, accessing financial records, or initiating payments. That makes a mistaken instruction or compromised login more consequential than a bad answer about a bank balance.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency has since issued AI examiner guidance that addresses outside agents, payment controls, and human approval. The framework is nonbinding and does not itself create new requirements for banks.

Citi's language does not automatically eliminate consumer fraud protections. Under U.S. federal consumer protection rules, banks generally must investigate unauthorized electronic transfers and limit customers' financial liability for fraud. Those protections cannot simply be waived through a banking agreement, although their application to transactions performed by customer-authorized AI agents remains less clear.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says banks cannot use agreements to waive those legal protections, although the rules distinguish theft by an outsider from transfers actually authorized by a customer or someone given access.

Whether a particular AI-related loss qualifies as unauthorized depends on how the transaction occurred.

PNC's updated agreement takes a stricter operational approach: Customers may use certain connection methods approved by the bank, but cannot give third-party AI agents their passwords or one-time security codes, and agents generally cannot initiate payments unless PNC expressly permits it.

#4916. This 108-Year-Old’s Daily Routine Includes 2 Easy Leg Exercises You Can Do at Home

Susan Young Browne, who still lives independently, begins every morning with this movement.

Earlier this year, Susan Young Browne from Delaware celebrated her 108th birthday—the news of which travelled across the world. Everyone wanted to know the retired teacher’s longevity secrets. How did Susan, who had just renewed her driving license until 2033, retain such a good quality of life?

Well, movement, it seems, has played an integral part. Firstly, Susan, who still walks unassisted, told TODAY that she continues to attend chair dancing classes at a local community centre.

But she’s also committed to consistent, everyday movement.

Susan begins every morning with a 10-minute stretching, strengthening, and balancing routine.

With flexibility, mobility, strength and balance all being key markers of longevity, Susan’s routine is a reminder that workouts do not need to be long and complicated to have far-reaching benefits.

Another key part of Susan’s daily exercise routine that likely contributes to her impressive healthspan (the number of years spent living in good health and free from chronic disease)? Her focus on leg strength.

“I get up and stand against the wall and exercise my legs. I make sure my legs are exercised,” Susan told TODAY.

Not only do strong legs help us move freely and reduce fall risk, but a growing body of evidence also points to an association between lower-body strength and cognitive function—another key element of longevity.

One oft-cited study found that older adults with greater leg strength had 34% lower odds of low cognitive function than those with weaker legs. Meanwhile, a 10-year study of more than 300 twin sisters reported “a striking protective relationship” between leg power and cognition. The twin with greater leg power at the beginning of the study maintained their cognitive function better and showed fewer age-related brain changes over the following decade.

While the exact mechanisms behind this association remain unclear, among scientists’ hypotheses are that stronger muscles may improve blood flow to the brain, that resistance training may influence nervous system function, and that lower-body strength can help preserve walking speed and mobility—both of which have been associated with a lower risk of dementia.

Using a wall for support, Susan can be seen balancing on one leg, which is a simple, effective, single-leg exercise that supports strength and balance.

Another simple move that only requires a wall? As the name suggests, a wall sit.

“Defined as an isometric exercise—an exercise where the working muscle doesn’t change length during the exercise and the joint doesn’t move—wall sits are super safe to perform, and put very little stress on the spine,” personal trainer Aimee Victoria Long previously explained to Women’s Health.

Mainly targeting the quadriceps (the muscles at the front of your thigh that support knee stability and everyday functional movements such as walking, getting up from a chair, and climbing stairs), wall sits can also improve endurance, balance, core, and lower-back strength.

Another simple, no-equipment exercise that supports functional lower-body strength is the humble bodyweight squat. Plus, one study even found that doing 60 seconds of squatting exercises during long periods of sitting may help preserve cognitive function.

Hannah Bradfield is a Senior Health and Fitness Writer for Women’s Health UK. #4913. Ethereum’s Glamsterdam upgrade could slip to May 2027 over compatibility concerns

Ethereum developers are weighing changes to gas pricing proposals that could disrupt existing smart contracts, after contacting at least 50 affected companies.

Ethereum’s Glamsterdam upgrade could be pushed back as far as May 2027 if developers decide to modify its specifications to address smart contract compatibility issues, according to discussions at Thursday’s All Core Developers meeting.

Glamsterdam is a planned Ethereum hard fork aimed at increasing the network’s capacity and efficiency. However, blockchain security firm ChainSecurity warned in October that proposed changes to Ethereum’s gas pricing could disrupt existing smart contracts and potentially expose them to exploitation, prompting developers to postpone the Hoodi testnet fork, originally scheduled for Oct. 26.

The concerns center on gas repricing proposals EIP-8037 and EIP-8038. Researchers identified 13 real-world examples of potentially affected contracts in October, while a November investigation examined eight smart contract invariants that could be disrupted by the upgrade.

During Thursday’s meeting, developers said the Ethereum Foundation, ChainSecurity and security firm Dedaub had collectively contacted at least 50 affected companies. Three projects were classified as high impact, with fixes completed or expected by mid-December, while medium-impact projects reported timelines extending to Jan. 10.

Developers debated whether to retain Glamsterdam’s existing specifications or modify them to reduce compatibility risks, as changes intended to protect some contracts could disrupt others.

“Every spec change could, again, break new invariants that we are not aware of breaking yet,” one developer warned during the meeting.

Under the current specifications, mainnet activation could come as early as mid-January 2027. However, waiting until January to decide could push activation to late February or early March, or April or May if modifications are adopted, and no decision has been reached yet.

Related: Vitalik ‘pivots’ ETH to store of value, crypto suffers after US midterms: Hodler’s Digest

Separately, Ethereum’s next planned hard fork, Hegotá, could see its scope reduced as the network seeks to accelerate its transition to post-quantum cryptography.

During the meeting, developers considered postponing some Ethereum Improvement Proposals to prioritize post-quantum features, although several argued that reducing the upgrade’s scope would offer little benefit unless it also shortened the rollout timeline.

Developers also raised compatibility concerns over EIP-8151, a proposal designed to protect accounts migrating to post-quantum security. A preliminary review identified a potentially large number of existing smart contracts that could be affected by the changes, complicating the proposal’s inclusion in Hegotá.

No decision was reached on Hegotá’s scope, with client teams expected to submit their positions ahead of further discussions in two weeks.

#4912. 7 Best Massage Guns for Muscle Recovery, Tested by Fitness Editors

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Looking for a new massage gun to incorporate into your routine? Here are your best bets.

A MASSAGE GUN can be instrumental in creating a lasting and regular recovery routine at home. As someone whose job involves working out almost every day, bringing recovery into my daily life has been huge in keeping me moving toward my goals. I like to use them to activate my legs to make the most out of sprint sessions and provide therapy after heavy lifting sessions. But they're not only great for athletes or fitness buffs; a massage gun can help anyone relieve sore muscles, improve circulation, and mitigate stiffness after tough workouts.

I have a few members of my family who regularly steal my massage gun to address stiffness or aches while watching Netflix or between Zoom calls at their desk. Massage guns are way more compact than foam rollers and pack way more of a punch when it comes to targeting your muscles. Plus, most models are compact enough for on-the-go use, making them great for travel or just tossed into your gym bag.

"There’s plenty of research to show massage guns have the ability to increase mobility, decrease pain and soreness, and improve overall performance," says Renato Sanchez, PT, DPT, CSCS, a physical therapist for the Real Salt Lake soccer club in the MLS. "It won’t be the fix-all tool to dramatically improve your health, but it will be a valuable supplement to your routine," Sanchez adds.

But let's be real: The massage gun market has become totally saturated. And with so many options out there, it's hard to decipher which ones are actually worth your hard-earned cash. (Although if you really want to save some dough, you can attempt to turn a jigsaw into a massage gun.) While there are certainly some great budget massage guns, you have to be careful with what you choose.

With specific recovery routines and preferences in mind, our guide of massage guns represents some of the best options on the market right now—including a deep dive into our top-tested models from Theragun and Hyperice, the two most popular massage gun brands out there.

Discover why we love each percussion massage gun model below, then keep scrolling to read advice from our experts on what to look for and the best practices for use. Note that different companies refer to the speed as percussions per minute, shortened to PPMs, or revolutions per minute, shortened to RPMs. They mean the same thing, but for this story we use PPMs.

This is the massage gun that I keep at my desk both at home and at the office. That's because it offers noiseless performance and doesn't take up much space at all. The cost is less than most of its rivals in the space, and it packs as much of a punch as the full-sized models of both top brands.

This lightweight device weighs only 1.6 pounds, so it won't sit like a rock in your gym bag (or make your arms quake post-upper body lift). This also means you can easily grip and move it around your body without tiring out your arms. Hyperice markets this as a travel device, which it can be, but when it comes to taking up less room in your carry-on bag, the Theragun Mini (below) can't be beat.

The Hypervolt Go 3 is the update to the Hypervolt Go 2, which I was also a fan of. This update keeps what was great, and features small improvements, like a redesigned massage head that hits more surface area than the previous generations. This improvement goes across the new Hypervolt 3 line.

The device is fully charged when you take it out of the box, so all you need to do is hold down the power button to get rolling. It has three different percussion speeds and two different head attachments to vary your experience, so it's nearly as customizable as more premium models (you get two more percussion speed settings with the Hypervolt 3 Pro). Best of all, the motor on this machine is extremely quiet, which allows me to use it in scenarios where sound could be an issue.

As someone who leads a busy, on-the-go lifestyle and travels a lot, I've never utilized a massage gun as much as this compact one. Its scaled-down size and lightweight design make it practical to chuck in my carry-on, backpack, or gym/work bag, so I bring it out of the house with me nearly every day.

Despite its smaller size, this massage gun's performance stands out, delivering a powerful massage experience that's comparable to its larger counterparts. It weighs less than 1.5 pounds, has 150 minutes of battery life, three different speed settings, and three attachment heads, so you're not missing out on much that bigger models may offer. I will say, however, it does deliver a slightly more surface-level massage than the Theragun PRO (which I used before acquiring the Mini). That being said, the power and depth offered by the Mini is plenty for most people to reap the benefits of percussion therapy.

"This is hands-down my favorite massage gun. its small enough that I can travel with it anywhere, and despite its odd shape, I find it easy to hold and use," says Samuel. "It’s my go-to for loosening chest and IT bands."

For those interested in adding a few premium features, I've also tested the Theragun Mini Plus, which provides heat to the treatment area. And regardless of the need for heat application for better recovery in your case, it does provide a pleasant experience. I wouldn’t say it is necessary for the price, and this original design can’t be beat.

My only qualm with this thing is that it's noise level is a limiting factor in terms of where I actually use it. It's compact and lightweight enough to bring on-the-go, but it's definitely not quiet enough to use in a subdued office setting, for example. It's quieter than larger models, but not as dampened as you'd think for one so small.

This massage gun from Renpho is one of the most popular purchases on Amazon and we can see why. With four interchangeable massage heads and five speed settings, this sub-$100 device competes with the likes of Hyperice and Therabody for pennies on the dollar.

Featuring a minimalist, ergonomic design, this massage gun feels comfortable and manageable in my hand, targeting everything from my traps to calves. The motor is powerful, delivering a massage that falls somewhere between the Hypervolt 3 and the Theragun PRO in terms of intensity.

Its battery life also impressed me, but the charging itself took a little bit longer than other models on the market. Whether you're looking for an entry-level massage gun to test the waters or want to purchase a spare to leave at the office, this one is a no-brainer in terms of overall value.

For anyone looking for a suitably powerful and quiet full-sized model, this is the way to go. Sure, there is the standard Hypervolt 3, but for a little more money, you can get two additional power settings, which means more options when it comes to your treatment. And if you want something that packs slightly less of a punch and is more mobile, the Hypervolt 3 Go is a much better pick.

The max power level on this gun is less than others on the list, but I don't count that as a negative. Instead, the additional power settings allow you to access lower levels than other devices, which will be welcomed by many users like me.

For the variability and the performance that this massage gun delivers, the weight is very reasonable. The handle is easy to grip and gives you good stability when you want to dig into the muscles a little deeper.

Read More: Normatec Elite Compression Boots Review

The Theragun Prime Plus includes a 120-minute battery life, heated attachment, and a multi-grip handle that makes hard-to-reach areas more accessible. There are quite a few Theraguns on the market right now, and I've tested them all. Choosing between the many full-sized options can be difficult, but in my opinion, this is the standout amongst the crowd.

For the percussive force it distributes, the weight is surprisingly light. The unique design allows me to change up my grip however I wish. And unlike other premium options, it's light enough for you to actually handle it with each grip. The heated attachment provides comfort during your treatment, and while its warmth may not actually be scientifically proven to be effective in this application, it is pleasant during use.

Like the other higher-end Theragun models, the Prime Plus also has “smart” capabilities with the Therabody app, which allows users to track progress and data with Bluetooth connectivity. With four attachments, plus five different percussion settings with up to 60 pounds of force, this massager leaves nothing to be desired.

Ekrin has entered the world of massage gun devices and quickly made a noticeable splash. This powerful massager has a sleekly designed handle that looks basic but more than gets the job done. It's easy to use, and comes with six different massage heads to target muscle groups in different ways.

Our Health Director Marty Munson finds the ergonomic design impressive. "I have joint issues in my hands, but this grip is really comfortable," says Munson. "I've used many of the mainstay models out there, but I'm impressed with how good this one is."

The device also has six different speed settings and a rechargeable battery, which provides up to 8 hours of use on a single charge. It also delivers up to 3,500 percussions per minute, meaning it's a good option if power is toward the top of your massage gun must-haves list.

The Rally Orbital Massager stands out as a versatile and effective new tool in recovery, which is why it earned a spot in our Men’s Health Fitness Awards. Its ergonomic design fits comfortably in the hand, making it easy to maneuver across different muscle groups. The device offers multiple intensity levels, allowing you to customize the massage experience based on your specific needs, whether it’s for post-workout recovery or general tension relief.

Samuel is a fan, finding this device gentler than other options and perhaps more appropriate for a larger segment of the population. Even at higher intensities, the device operates with minimal noise, making it suitable for use in shared spaces or while watching TV. The battery life is also pretty solid.

Overall, the Rally Orbital Massager delivers excellent value for anyone seeking an accessible at-home massage solution, and manages to bring more innovation to a space that has been advancing for years. Its combination of thoughtful design, strong performance, and user-friendly features makes it a standout choice among other premium products.

To learn more about what to look for in a massage gun, we spoke with Vinh Pham, PT, a physical therapist and the founder of Myodetox, a manual therapy and movement clinic with locations in Canada and the U.S. According to Pham, the three most important things are reliability, noise, and battery life. "I need something that I know is well-made and won’t malfunction during operation, especially because I’m using it on injured athletes. Noise is the next most important factor. I need to be able to talk to my athletes over the noise of the gun without yelling at them."

Keeping treatment quiet is a major priority. "Personally, noise to me is number one," says Pham. "I want to be able to use the massage guns in public, and having it sound like a power tool would make it unusable." This is a feeling that I also agree with; especially when treating yourself around other people, you can feel self-conscious.

Next up is battery life, as PTs and athletes can’t have guns dying in the middle of treatment. Pham says that he expects a massage gun to last several full days without requiring a charge. "You’ll also want to be able to throw the gun in your bag or take it on a weekend trip without worrying about finding an outlet," Pham says.

Given the fact that massage guns are required to vibrate intensely in order to get the job done, it's not the kind of product you want to be sent with loose screws. Given how much the market has grown in recent years, there have been a lot of knockoff brands releasing subpar models that won't go the distance. Hands-on experience, like our team at Men's Health focuses on, is important in the research process. All of our picks have been vetted for durability, but it comes as no surprise that if you want the best and a brand name you can trust, you should expect to spend a little more.

Sufficient speed, or percussions per minute (PPM), plays a role in how the gun promotes blood flow. The higher the percussive rate, the more it can stimulate circulation. Look for a massage gun with a high percussive force and adjustable speed settings so you can deliver adequate force to different muscles. Another factor to consider is amplitude, which describes the amount of distance the massage head travels back and forth. This controls how effectively you can target certain muscle groups and how deeply the massager can get into the muscle tissue.

Just as important as amplitude is the gun's stall force, or the amount of pressure that the motor can apply to the muscle before it stops working. The higher the stall force, the more powerful a massage the gun can put out. Remember, though, that a massage gun shouldn't necessarily attack your muscles. In fact, for most people, less force is more. So don't get overly caught up in having the most "powerful" gun on the market; you likely won't need it to gain recovery benefits.

Different attachments can provide different massage techniques and sensations that may be suitable for different muscles. Many massage guns tout a host of attachments, but realize this: You'll likely just use a handful of these (or sometimes, your favorite one). So don't get deluded into purchasing because of multiple attachments. Once you've purchased your massage gun, be sure to properly research what attachments are effective for what muscles. Using the wrong attachment can dramatically alter the effectiveness of the massage gun.

A portable and lightweight massage gun is ideal, especially if you plan to use it on the go or travel with it. Consider the weight, size, and the case included.

Of course, even the best guns leave room for improvement. Some options come with convenient travel cases and charging stands—something Pham would like to see more products offer. He also mentions that dishwasher-safe attachment heads would make for easier cleaning. And, as the market continues to progress, he hopes for smaller (yet still powerful) designs and Bluetooth app integration.

As the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, part of my job is to evaluate the latest and greatest recovery gear available. I've used massage guns regularly for the past decade for muscle activation and post-training recovery. The testing pool for this list started with dozens of models across a range of price points, including the bestselling brands, both established and new. I tested each for several weeks, in multiple scenarios, including at home and at the gym.

In addition to my own testing, this guide was made with input and testing notes from other knowledgeable Men's Health editors, including MH Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., and Senior Fitness Editor Brett Williams, NASM. We consulted with respected physical therapists like Vinh Pham, PT, at Myodetox and Renato Sanchez for expert advice. We evaluated each device for durability, effectiveness, ergonomics (for ease of use), and portability. We also considered price point, as many massage guns offer better overall value than others.

After all this testing and research, we found these massage guns that we recommend.

Sanchez recommends first asking yourself why you’re considering a massage gun. "What are you looking to get out of one? Is it for recovery, pain relief, or helping you reach your fitness goals? If you answered yes to any of those, then you might be a good candidate to add one to your shopping cart," he explains.

"Massage guns can be used as an alternative to the foam roller as a self-myofascial release tool," adds Pham. He notes that benefits include everything from decreased stress, pain, and tissue tension to enhanced recovery, blood circulation, and range of motion.

"You can use it pre-workout to warm up the muscles and post-workout to decrease tightness and soreness," says Pham.

You don’t want to spend hours upon hours using your massage gun. Instead, you’ll want to spend 90 to 120 seconds on any given muscle group, floating the gun across that area, according to Samuel. "Aim to follow the direction of the muscle fibers. That means running your gun across your chest, from the center toward your shoulder, instead of running it up and down your chest."

But be mindful to not run your massage gun across joints; you want to keep it focused on the soft tissue only. "And don’t try to aggressively drive the gun deep into the muscle, expecting more 'relief.' Using a massage gun shouldn’t hurt," explains Samuel.

Want to learn more on how you should be using one of these buzzy tools? Check out our how-to-use massage guns guide for instructions for best practices before, during, and after workouts.

Massage guns have gained a lot of popularity in recent years as a tool for muscle recovery—but do they really work? The blunt answer is they can. But it all depends on how, when, and where you use them.

These massagers offer rapid, percussive strokes designed to penetrate the muscle tissue, stimulate blood flow, and help break up adhesions. The research on the effectiveness of massage guns for muscle recovery is promising, but still limited.

A study published in the Journal of Clinical and Diagnostic Research found that using a massage gun on the quadriceps muscles after exercise resulted in a significant reduction in muscle soreness and an increase in muscle flexibility compared to a control group. Another study found that using a massage gun after exercise improved blood flow to the muscles and reduced muscle fatigue.

So, they can help with muscle soreness with correct use, but shouldn't be used as a replacement for other recovery methods such as rest, proper nutrition, active stretching, and dynamic mobility work.

We asked Sanchez how folks can get to those hard-to-reach areas with their massage guns. Here's his take: "Massage guns mainly target superficial muscles making it hard to isolate deeper musculature. Therefore, yes, the location of muscles can impact the effectiveness of this modality.

I think it’s safe to say the majority of people can reach the front side of their bodies using a massage gun, but you’ll need decent shoulder mobility if you’re looking to target the mid and low back. That’s when you’d want to get a massage gun that is more ergonomic or can be adjusted.

If mobility is a limiting factor, you may consider trading the massage gun for a lacrosse ball for pinpoint contact. Sometimes you might just be better off asking a friend, what’s the saying … I’ll scratch your back if you scratch mine?"

Charles Thorp is the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he shares the best product recommendations in gym equipment, recovery tools, supplements, and more. #4911. Rosie Huntington-Whiteley Uses Banded Chin-Ups to Build Upper-Body Strength

The supermodel’s go-to move targets your back and arms.

Rosie Huntington-Whiteley returned to the Victoria's Secret runway this year after a 16-year hiatus, but the supermodel has continued to make fitness a priority throughout her career.

“It’s really about consistency because I’m a gym girl—I’m always training and taking care of myself,” Rosie told Vogue.

The former Burberry Body face has previously cited strength training as her main form of exercise.

“I feel really strong and it's improved my posture, muscle tone, and definition,” she said to Vogue on a separate occasion.

She recently shared a workout clip of herself doing an impressive upper-body exercise—the banded chin-up—just days before the show, writing: “No days off.”

Chin-ups are a compound exercise targeting your back and arm muscles, including the latissimus dorsi (lats), biceps, and trapezius (traps).

A chin-up uses an underhand grip, with your palms facing you, while a pull-up uses an overhand grip, with your palms facing away.

Using a thicker band gives you more assistance when performing reps, while a thinner band gives you less.

Remember: while models' and celebrities' training routines can be inspiring, genetics also play a significant role in body shape, height and how easily someone builds muscle or stays lean. Take inspiration from the healthy habits – not the expectation of looking identical.

While the chin-up is a challenging movement, you can build up to your first bodyweight rep—without a band—using a few progression exercises.

Holding yourself above the bar keeps your muscles under constant tension, which helps build strength.

This exercise requires you to lower yourself as slowly as possible from the top of the movement. People are generally much stronger in the lowering phase of an exercise than in the lifting portion, making it easier than trying to pull yourself up. However, the movement still works your muscles throughout the entire range of motion, helping you build the strength needed to perform a chin-up.

Rosie has highlighted the importance of focusing on skill and feeling confident over aesthetics.

“For me, it’s really about feeling strong and fit, as opposed to thinking about a number on the scales or on a measuring tape. Competence builds confidence,” she said.

Getting stronger brings her a sense of accomplishment.

“There's nothing more satisfactory to me than when I go up in weight,” she added to Vogue. “It makes me happy when I start to see the results of [consistently] lifting.” In fact, regularly working out is “when [she] feels her strongest and fittest.”

She added that motherhood had given her a new perspective on her body.

“I’m about to turn 40 next year; I look at my body and I have so much appreciation for having had two children,” Rosie continued.

#4910. Trump’s SEC nominee Johnson backs formal rulemaking for tokenized stock trading

Former CFTC Commissioner and Democrat Kristin Johnson and ex-SEC aide Steven Levine appeared before lawmakers Thursday.

President Donald Trump’s nominees to fill two vacancies at the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) faced questions about investor protections, regulatory oversight and financial innovation during a Senate confirmation hearing Thursday, including scrutiny of the agency’s approach to tokenized securities.

Kristin Johnson, Trump’s Democratic nominee, backed formal rulemaking to address concerns about the agency’s exemption for tokenized stock trading.

“I feel strongly that regulation is made better through the notice and comment period,” Johnson told the Senate Banking Committee in response to Democratic Senator Angela Alsobrooks. She added that she would welcome the opportunity to address issues covered by the exemption through that process.

The SEC’s Sept. 17 exemption lets qualifying platforms trade blockchain-based versions of US-listed shares without registering as securities exchanges under certain conditions. The order took effect immediately and invites comments on possible changes.

Johnson, a former Commodity Futures Trading Commission commissioner, appeared alongside Republican Steven Levine, a former aide to SEC Commissioner Mark Uyeda. If confirmed, they would bring the five-member commission to four members, with three Republicans and one Democrat.

The hearing comes as the SEC has scaled back enforcement activity and pursued regulatory changes intended to accommodate digital assets, including efforts to facilitate tokenized securities that have drawn scrutiny from lawmakers and market participants.

The measure has drawn objections from publicly traded companies, with 67 opposing the tokenization of their shares on the OKXICE platform, according to a Nov. 5 public notice.

Johnson also cited concerns about Anti-Money Laundering and Know Your Customer compliance, noting that objections to the exemption extended beyond investor protection.

Levine, meanwhile, said he had not closely studied the innovation exemption but understood it to be time-limited and include investor protections. He emphasized that Congress had authorized the SEC to grant exemptions from federal securities laws when doing so serves the public interest and remains consistent with investor protection requirements.

He pointed to exchange-traded funds as an example of financial innovation that initially developed through regulatory exemptions before becoming subject to broader agency rules.

Related: Robinhood’s Tenev warns US tokenization uncertainty deters ‘serious assets’

If confirmed, Johnson would become the SEC’s only Democratic commissioner, a development some in the crypto industry believe could strengthen the agency’s approach to regulation.

“Crypto isn’t a partisan issue, and the rules that come out of a bipartisan commission will stand on firmer footing,” Jessica Martinez, US policy director at digital asset infrastructure company Fireblocks, told Cointelegraph.

Martinez added that even minority commissioners can influence policy by challenging proposals and pushing for unresolved issues to be addressed before rules are finalized.

Senators have until noon Friday to submit additional written questions to the nominees, with responses due by 5:00 pm ET on Nov. 24, according to the committee’s closing remarks.

The nominations could then advance to a committee vote before being considered by the full Senate. Both nominees would require Senate confirmation before taking their seats at the SEC.

#4909. Danielle Frankel Reimagines the 21st Century Bridal Store

After nearly 10 years in business, fashion designer Danielle Frankel Hirsch has opened a 12,000-square-foot location in Tribeca with interiors set to change the bridal game. To create the new space, which opened in early November, Frankel Hirsch worked with AD PRO Directory designer Augusta Hoffman and Studio Partners Architecture.

The nearly two-year design process is complete, and the Danielle Frankel bridal salon is now ready for appointments. “We’re finally at the point where my heart and my head have been,” says Frankel Hirsch, who worked with Hoffman on her previous Los Angeles boutique and New York City atelier. “Because this is our third space together, we can almost speak in shorthand now.”

Frankel Hirsch on the staircase wearing a shirt she designed from Fortuny fabric. Hoffman used the same Fortuny print throughout the space for wrapping side tables, keepsake boxes on the shelves, as well as for the woven seats on barstools.

The unassuming entrance to Danielle Frankel on Hudson Street

In the reception room just inside the street entrance, the desk is custom, the chairs are antique, and the custom pendant is by Jamb.

Hoffman worked with the artist Miriam Ellner to create eglomise paneling surrounding the staircase. “The eglomise is one of my favorite things because when we were working with the artist we worked so intimately with her,” Frankel Hirsch says. “We worked on the placement the way that we do our laces. We kept going back and forth with the drawings because I wanted it to feel like our lace placement.”

On a recent morning, a bride and her wedding party were busy in the VIP suite making a final selection. The beaming group entered the space through an unassuming brown storefront entrance on Harrison Street, its two large glass windows encased in a sheer linen. From there they ascended a staircase up to a large gallery with over 30-foot floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking the streets below on two sides, and a hand-painted mural pattern above on the ceiling.

The interiors of the original 19th-century Queen Anne–style red brick building were transformed by Hoffman (full disclosure: I am writing Hoffman’s design monograph publishing with Rizzoli in Fall 2027) into a modern, elegant bridal boutique that honors the history of the original New York Mercantile Exchange, first established in the 1880s to keep the standards of the grocer business. “We wanted the space to stay pretty bright and focus on the architecture, but we needed a lot of seating,” Hoffman says. “There was a lot of pressure because we wanted it to feel like Danielle and we wanted to leave our mark on the space, but it’s also so beautiful as is and we didn’t want to have too many interventions that take away from that.”

The rug, vintage Dutch leather armchairs, and custom clothing racks create one of the four seated zones in the gallery area. The wall features antique mottled glass windows. “We wanted this wall to feel historically accurate,” Hoffman says.

The custom oak screen features shelves for displaying miniature gowns by Danielle Frankel. The shelves are lined in silver leaf. The antique stool is reupholstered in a Fortuny fabric.

The view of the gallery area from a second floor bridal suite. The vintage teak seating set is reupholstered in a fabric by Manuel Canovas and the glass cocktail tables and Fortuny wrapped side tables are custom. The custom window panels are by Augusta Hoffman Studio for Wovn Home and the custom curtain hardware are bronze leaves designed by Hoffman. Hoffman pulled the leaf design from the details on the columns.

What previously functioned as a large, open space with a small mezzanine, had little existing infrastructure–no electrical, HVAC, or plumbing—and is now an area where brides can plot as they make the most important decision for their wedding day. In the gallery, Hoffman created distinct zones where wedding parties wait before their appointment in a private fitting room.

Much of the furniture was sourced by Hoffman and Frankel Hirsch together on trips to Paris. Antique glass vitrines separate the space, which they included from the previous New York gallery and filled with Frankel Hirsch’s own family wedding photos as well as printed details brides can use for their fitting. One vitrine has a board layered with references of crinoline and interlining. Another has custom Danielle Frankel cufflinks. An oak folding screen lines one half of the room, with miniature gowns set on shelves lined in silver leaf paper. Custom parchment and cerused oak racks Hoffman designed to withstand the weight of a wedding dress line the floor displaying roughly 65 dresses from Danielle Frankel collections.

The reflection of the wall is seen in the mirrored structure designed to house the elevator bank and stairwell to the street entrance. A framed antique floral plaster relief is flanked with 1930s Italian wall sconces in patinated glass and metal.

The staircase and elevator bank within the mirrored structure. “We had to add the elevator for function and for code, and we were like ‘How do we take this existing architecture and put an elevator in the middle of the room?’” Hoffman says. “It feels super unexpected, versus trying to hide it, and you get to see more of the surrounding architecture and light in the reflection.”

The custom rug is topped with an antique stool upholstered in a Fortuny fabric, a 1950s chair, and a 19th-century English pine console table.

The view from the sitting area adjacent to a bar. The vintage teak seating set was among the first items Hoffman and Frankel Hirsch sourced for the space. The custom bar stool is woven with a Fortuny fabric.

The view from within the staircase to the gallery area. The custom center table is by Rafael Carneiro Triboli and the French chairs are from the 1930s.

Hoffman and Studio Partners Architects took what was formerly the mezzanine, originally separated from the below with only a single-bar metal railing, and made it into a full wall with antiqued mottled glass windows. In the center they constructed a cascading grand staircase, cleverly concealing the stockroom underneath, which leads upstairs to three private bridal suites. The hallways, painted in Wenge by Benjamin Moore, lead to the bridal suites, each designed differently and filled with antique and vintage furniture, custom carpets, lighting, and racks. The walls are painted in Presidente Roman Clay by Portola Paints, an earthy contrast to the white and ivory dresses, which are naturally the center of attention for visitors in each room.

When guests are finished in their suites, there’s a bar in the gallery space where wedding parties can sit and make the final selection. The wedding party that morning had selected the dress and were toasting champagne to celebrate. “It’s just as much about the hospitality and the warmth as it is about the gowns,” Frankel Hirsch says.

In the VIP bridal suite, which can be accessed through a discreet entrance on Harrison Street, the custom sofa is upholstered in Holland & Sherry’s Corbel in Henna. The artwork features fragments of 19th century Japanese brocade.

The midcentury armchairs are upholstered in a Watts 1874 fabric and flank a vintage oak table.

The rack, mirror, and ceiling pendant are all custom in the VIP bridal suite.

In the dressing area of the VIP bridal suite, the ceiling pendant is custom and the closet wall covering is by Watts 1874.

The 1930s lounge chair is reupholstered in a Fortuny fabric and the 1970s lamp is from Brazil.

#4908. A Better Airport Outfit Starts With the Basics

We're making a case for putting a little more thought into your travel outfit.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Airports can be a bit intimidating. You’ve got the TSA line to worry about, but more importantly, you have your outfit to figure out. Unfortunately, some people judge what you’re wearing while traveling (it’s me, I’m people). But I also don’t think looking presentable has to be that hard. Some guys show up in full sweats, looking like they're about to spend the next six hours in bed. Others dress like they're heading straight from baggage claim to a dinner reservation. Personally, I think there's a happy medium somewhere in there. You should be comfortable enough to sleep through your flight, but you also shouldn't have to change your entire outfit the second you land. From comfortable pants and breathable T-shirts to stylish sneakers, these are the essentials worth packing for your next flight.

And while I love a good matching sweatsuit as much as the next guy, there are plenty of other ways to dress comfortably for the airport. We’ve got stretchy trousers that look pretty darn good, a solid pair of sneakers, and layers that work alone or together. It's about finding clothes that do a little bit of everything, especially if you like to travel light.

If you’re looking to spruce up your fit for your next flight (and to become someone’s airport crush), here’s what to know.

I'm not saying you can't wear jeans on a plane, but why would you when you have so many more comfortable alternatives? You'll be sitting for hours, probably in a seat that doesn't give you much room to move, so the last thing you want is a waistband digging into your stomach. Look for pants with a little stretch, breathable fabrics, and a relaxed fit that won't feel restrictive when you're sitting down. Brands like Vuori and DUER have gotten particularly good at making pants that feel like loungewear without necessarily looking like it. And if you're committed to sweatpants, that's perfectly fine, too. Just go for a pair with a cleaner, more structured fit.

Reigning Champ Midweight Terry Relaxed Sweatpant

You really don't need to overthink your airport T-shirt. A good cotton tee will do just fine, especially if it's something you already wear regularly. Personally, I'd avoid anything too tight or made from a heavy fabric, since airports and airplanes can get surprisingly stuffy. A slightly relaxed fit gives you more room to move and makes layering easier, too. I tend to gravitate toward simple, solid-colored tees because they go with practically anything. Uniqlo's AIRism Cotton Oversized T-Shirt is a good example of something that's affordable, comfortable, and easy to dress up or down depending on what else you're wearing.

I don't care if you're flying to Miami in the middle of July; bring a sweatshirt. Airplane cabins have a habit of feeling like refrigerators, and I'd much rather have an extra layer than spend an entire flight shivering. A good crewneck or hoodie is probably all you need, preferably something soft that isn't too bulky to stuff into your bag when you're not wearing it. I'm partial to oversized sweatshirts for traveling, though you don't need to go so big that you're drowning in fabric. Something like Alo's Accolade Crewneck works well because you can wear it with sweatpants or a nicer pair of trousers. And honestly, if you're desperate, a sweatshirt can always double as a makeshift pillow.

Abercrombie SwEssential Popover 2.0 Hoodie

Todd Snyder Champion Relaxed French Terry Crewneck

Eddie Bauer Micro Polar Fleece Lined Pullover Hoodie

Depending on where you're headed, a lightweight jacket might be one of the more useful things you bring. I'm not talking about a huge puffer or anything that'll take up half your carry-on. Think windbreakers, chore jackets, and lightweight layers that you can easily throw over a T-shirt or sweatshirt. If you're traveling somewhere with unpredictable weather, a technical jacket from Patagonia or Arc'teryx makes sense. Otherwise, a simple chore jacket from somewhere like Quince or Gap can make an otherwise basic airport outfit look a little more put-together. Plus, you'll probably wear it during the trip anyway, so it's one less thing to pack.

Quince 100% Organic Herringbone Twill Shirt Jacket

Between getting to the airport, navigating security, and walking what feels like three miles to your gate, you'll probably spend more time on your feet than you realize. That's why I'd prioritize comfortable sneakers over anything else when putting together an airport outfit. You want a pair with good cushioning, enough support, and ideally something easy to slip on and off. New Balance, Hoka, and On all make sneakers that fit the bill, though I'd stick with a pair you've already broken in rather than trying something new on travel day. And since you're probably only bringing one or two pairs of shoes on your trip, bonus points if they match the rest of your wardrobe.

You really don't need much here. In fact, I'd argue the best airport outfits are pretty simple. But a few accessories can make even a basic T-shirt-and-sweatpants combination feel more intentional. A classic Yankees cap from '47 is great for early flights when you don't feel like doing your hair, and a good pair of sunglasses is always useful when you're heading somewhere sunny. I also like wearing a watch when I travel, mostly because I don't want to keep pulling out my phone to check the time. None of these things are essential, obviously, but they're easy ways to make the outfit feel a little more like your own.

Seiko Analog Green Dial Automatic Silver Stainless Steel Watch
